scenario.context: The varsity basketball team is in the locker room after a close loss. The team captain, Marcus, missed the game-winning free throw in the final seconds. Coach Henderson is addressing the team while they change out of their uniforms.
scenario.text: Coach Henderson slams his clipboard against the bench. 'Marcus, that was unacceptable. You choked. I've told you a hundred times: you lack the mental toughness to close out games. You're too soft when the pressure is on.' Marcus looks down at his shoes, wiping sweat from his forehead. 'Coach, my ankle has been killing me all week. I couldn't feel my foot on that last shot; it just slipped.' Henderson waves a hand dismissively. 'Excuses, excuses! When I played point guard in '98, I sprained my wrist in the semifinals and still hit the game-winner. The difference is desire. You don't want it bad enough, plain and simple.'
scenario.speaker_context: Coach Henderson is a former player who prides himself on grit. He attributes his own past success despite injury to his character (desire), but attributes Marcus's failure despite injury to Marcus's character (softness), ignoring the situational factor of the ankle injury in both cases.

structure.pattern_description: Coach Henderson attributes Marcus's missed shot to an internal character flaw (lack of mental toughness/softness) while ignoring the situational constraint (severe ankle injury). Conversely, Henderson explains his own past success despite injury by citing his internal character (desire), failing to recognize the asymmetry in how he judges others versus himself.
structure.formal_form: Other person's negative outcome -> attributed to character trait. Own (or in-group) negative/outcome context -> attributed to situational factor or overcome by character. The observer ignores external constraints affecting the actor.
structure.why_wrong: The coach dismisses a clear physical limitation (the ankle injury) as an excuse, labeling it a character defect. He applies a double standard: his own injury was an obstacle he overcame through will, but Marcus's injury is irrelevant to the outcome and only serves to reveal weakness. This ignores the probability that the injury directly caused the mechanical failure of the shot.
structure.counterpoint: Mental toughness is a valid factor in sports. If Marcus had been fully healthy and still missed due to panic, the coach's assessment might be accurate. The error lies in automatically assuming character is the cause while ruling out the situational evidence (the injury) without verification.

assessment.identification_prompt: Coach Henderson is very quick to call Marcus 'soft.' But listen to how he describes his own experience with an injury in '98. How does his explanation for his own performance differ from how he explains Marcus's?

rubric.description: Player agrees with the coach that Marcus is simply soft and needs to try harder.
Player feels the coach is being mean to Marcus but cannot explain the logical inconsistency.
Player notices the coach is ignoring the ankle injury but does not connect it to how the coach explained his own past injury.
Player identifies the asymmetry: The coach blames Marcus's character for the miss despite injury, but credits his own character for succeeding despite injury, recognizing the unfair double standard.

Player explicitly names the fundamental attribution error, explains the actor-observer bias in the coach's reasoning, and suggests that the injury is a situational factor that needs to be evaluated before judging character.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: The coach says his injury in '98 didn't stop him because he had 'desire.' He says Marcus's injury doesn't matter because he lacks 'toughness.' If Marcus had made the shot despite the injury, would the coach call him tough, or would he say it was just luck?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly. The coach sees his own history through the lens of situation-plus-character, but sees Marcus only through the lens of character. Why do you think authority figures like coaches often fall into this trap when evaluating players under their command?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Coach Henderson is intense, old-school, and values 'grit' above all else. He is not cruel but is blind to his own cognitive biases, believing firmly that effort conquers all physical limitations.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: You think injuries matter? Injuries happen to everyone. The only thing that separates winners from losers is what's up here (taps temple). Marcus folded. That's a character issue.
game_hooks.resolution_path: If the player points out the inconsistency regarding the '98 game, Coach Henderson pauses, his brow furrowing. He mutters about how 'times were different,' then asks the trainer to check the severity of Marcus's ankle. Upon seeing the significant swelling, he grunts, admits he might have been hasty, and tells Marcus to ice it and review the film tomorrow.

scenario.context: The player visits the farming village of Greymoor, which has been hit by two consecutive bad harvests. The village council is debating whether to invest their remaining savings in a new irrigation system. Engineer Dalla has presented a detailed plan showing that the irrigation system would stabilize yields even in dry years, and the regional agricultural records show that three consecutive bad harvests have never occurred in two hundred years of record-keeping. But Elder Sorn, who lived through a famine as a child, dominates the discussion.
scenario.text: Elder Sorn grips the edge of the council table. 'Two bad harvests in a row. It will be three — I can feel it. And if we spend our savings on Dalla's pipes and ditches, we'll have nothing left when the third failure comes. No food, no coin, nothing. We should bury the gold, ration what grain we have, and pray.' Dalla responds calmly: 'Elder Sorn, the records show—' Sorn cuts her off. 'Records! The records didn't predict the last two failures either. Things are getting worse. The soil is dying. Even if we build the irrigation, something else will go wrong — it always does. A flood, a blight, locusts. We should prepare for the worst and hope I'm wrong.' Dalla looks to the player. 'The irrigation plan costs sixty percent of our reserves and produces returns within one season. Even in the worst drought on record, irrigated fields in the next valley yielded seventy percent of normal. But Elder Sorn sees only catastrophe.'
scenario.speaker_context: Elder Sorn is not stupid — he survived a real famine and his fear is rooted in genuine trauma. But his expectation of negative outcomes has detached from the evidence. He is overweighting the probability of continued disaster and underweighting the evidence for the irrigation system's effectiveness.

structure.pattern_description: Sorn systematically overestimates the likelihood of negative outcomes (three consecutive bad harvests, irrigation failure, additional disasters) while dismissing evidence of positive possibilities (historical base rates, irrigation data from the next valley, Dalla's engineering analysis). His trauma-driven expectation of catastrophe leads him to reject an investment that the evidence supports, preferring inaction and hoarding as the 'safe' choice — even though inaction carries its own risks.
structure.formal_form: Agent overestimates probability of negative outcomes P- and underestimates probability of positive outcomes P+, leading to risk-averse decisions that are not justified by the available evidence. Negative possibilities are treated as near-certainties; positive evidence is dismissed as unreliable or insufficient.
structure.why_wrong: The historical record shows no precedent for three consecutive failures. The irrigation data from a neighboring valley demonstrates effectiveness even in severe drought. Sorn dismisses both sources of evidence with vague catastrophizing ('something else will go wrong, it always does'). His plan — bury the gold and ration — actually increases the risk of famine by forgoing the investment that would stabilize food supply.
structure.counterpoint: Pessimism can be adaptive when the downside risk is catastrophic and irreversible. If spending the reserves on irrigation and having it fail would mean starvation with no recovery option, Sorn's caution has a rational kernel. The bias is in treating every possible negative outcome as likely while treating every positive outcome as unlikely, regardless of the evidence.

assessment.identification_prompt: Elder Sorn has real experience with famine, and his fear is understandable. But Dalla has data and a plan. What is driving Sorn's opposition — is it the evidence, or something else?

rubric.description: Player agrees with Sorn that things will get worse and the village should save its money.
Player thinks Sorn is being too cautious but attributes it to his personality rather than a cognitive pattern.
Player recognizes Sorn is overestimating the risk but does not connect it to the systematic underweighting of positive evidence.
Player identifies pessimism bias: Sorn overestimates negative outcomes and dismisses positive evidence, and his trauma is driving the distortion rather than the data.

Player identifies pessimism bias, explains how Sorn's trauma amplifies negative expectations beyond what evidence supports, recognizes that his 'safe' plan of inaction carries its own risks, and can articulate when caution is genuinely warranted versus when it is the bias talking.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Sorn says 'something else will go wrong — it always does.' Does it always? What does the two-hundred-year record actually show? And consider: if the village does nothing and a third bad harvest comes anyway, are they better or worse off than if they had built the irrigation?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Good. Now here is the tension: Sorn's pessimism comes from surviving a real famine. His fear is not irrational — it is disproportionate. How do you respect someone's lived experience while still pointing out that their fear is distorting their judgment? Is there a way to honour what Sorn knows without letting it dictate policy?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Elder Sorn is not a villain — he is a traumatized survivor whose protective instincts have calcified into reflexive catastrophizing. He speaks with quiet intensity and invokes his famine memories as moral authority. He is respected in the village, which makes his pessimism influential. Dalla is pragmatic, data-oriented, and frustrated but not dismissive of Sorn's experience.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Sorn fixes you with hollow eyes. 'You're young. You've never watched a village eat its seed grain because there was nothing else. I have. When I tell you it's going to get worse, I'm not guessing. I'm remembering.'
game_hooks.resolution_path: If the player identifies the pessimism bias, they can broker a compromise: invest in the irrigation system but keep a forty-percent reserve as Sorn's emergency fund. When the irrigation works and the next harvest comes in strong, Sorn admits he was wrong about the outcome — but adds, quietly, 'I'll never stop worrying. That's what surviving does to you.' The player gains the village's trust and access to Dalla's engineering workshop.

scenario.context: In the guild workshop of the bustling town of Ironforge, the master blacksmith and the apprentice are debating whether to commission a new set of enchanted hammers for the upcoming siege. The town has seen two recent battles where weapons failed due to unexpected magical interference. The guild council is torn between spending the majority of their funds on the hammers or saving the gold in case the next battle brings even worse setbacks.
scenario.text: Master Bronn slams his hammer on the anvil, eyes narrowed. "Two battles where our blades cracked under strange magic. The third will be the one that shatters us. If we pour our gold into those cursed hammers, we'll have nothing left when the next wave of sorcery hits. We should hoard what we have, ration the steel we own, and pray the enemy stays away." Apprentice Lyra steps forward, holding a parchment of recent experiments. "Master, the new enchantments have a 87% success rate in trials, and the kingdom's archives show only one instance of three consecutive magical failures in a century. The hammers could give us a decisive edge." Bronn cuts her off, voice shaking. "Archives! They never warned us about the last two failures. The world is getting darker. Even with enchanted hammers, another disaster—plague, fire, a dragon—will strike. We must prepare for the worst and hope I'm wrong."
scenario.speaker_context: Master Bronn is a seasoned veteran who survived a devastating siege as a youth. His fear is understandable, but his expectation of continual disaster has eclipsed the statistical evidence and the promising results of the new enchantments.

structure.pattern_description: Bronn systematically overestimates the likelihood of negative outcomes (a third catastrophic battle, failure of enchanted hammers, additional calamities) while dismissing evidence of positive possibilities (high success rate of enchantments, historical rarity of three consecutive failures). His trauma-driven expectation of catastrophe leads him to reject a potentially beneficial investment.
structure.why_wrong: Bronn is giving excessive weight to recent negative events and personal trauma, ignoring base‑rate data and the strong experimental success of the enchanted hammers. This overestimation of danger skews his decision‑making toward inaction and unnecessary risk avoidance.
structure.counterpoint: Consider the empirical success rate of the enchanted hammers and the historical rarity of three successive magical failures. Balancing recent fear with long‑term data can lead to a more rational investment decision.

assessment.identification_prompt: Which cognitive bias is Master Bronn displaying when he predicts another disaster despite the evidence supporting the enchanted hammers?

rubric.description: No recognition of bias; answer is unrelated or blank.
Identifies a bias but selects the wrong one (e.g., confirmation bias).
Names pessimism bias but provides an incomplete or inaccurate explanation.
Correctly names pessimism bias and partially explains how it appears in the dialogue.
Accurately names pessimism bias, fully explains the overestimation of negative outcomes, and connects it to Bronn's trauma and the ignored statistical evidence.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: A brief tutorial appears, showing how pessimism bias leads people to overweigh recent negative events and underweigh base‑rate data, using a side‑by‑side comparison of Bronn's statements versus the archival statistics.
assessment.follow_up_if_right: The player receives a confidence boost and unlocks a dialogue option to calmly present the trial data to Bronn, opening a path toward a constructive resolution.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Master Bronn is cautious, stoic, and heavily influenced by past trauma; he tends to expect the worst and values security over risk.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: ‘Two failures are a warning, not a guarantee. The world has grown darker…’
game_hooks.resolution_path: If the player presents the success statistics and acknowledges Bronn's fear, Bronn can be persuaded to allocate a portion of the funds to the enchanted hammers while keeping a reserve, leading to a successful siege outcome and increased guild reputation.

The Dustwalkers have completed forty-seven out of fifty contracts successfully over three years — a 94% success rate. But Venn is fixated on the three failures.
scenario.text: Guildmaster Venn tosses the contract renewal onto the table. 'I'm not signing this. The Dustwalkers lost an entire shipment of silkwood last autumn. Before that, they were late by two weeks on the dye delivery — two weeks! Cost us the Midsummer Fair orders. And the year before, they let a crate of glassware get smashed on the mountain pass. Three disasters in three years.' His trade secretary, Maren, clears her throat. 'Guildmaster, those are three incidents out of fifty contracts. The other forty-seven arrived on time and intact. Their reliability rate is ninety-four percent — higher than any other company we've used. The next best is the Ironwheel Guild at eighty-one percent.' Venn shakes his head. 'I don't care about the forty-seven. I remember the silkwood. I remember explaining to Lord Ashcroft why his glass was in pieces. The bad ones stick with you, Maren.'
scenario.speaker_context: Venn is not being irrational in isolation — each failure did cause real harm. But he is giving the three negative events disproportionate weight relative to the forty-seven positive ones, and he is about to make a decision that would replace a 94% reliable partner with an 81% reliable one.

structure.pattern_description: Venn's memory and emotional weighting are dominated by the three failures. He can recall each one vividly — the silkwood, the dye delay, the smashed glassware — but the forty-seven successes have faded into an undifferentiated background. The negative events carry disproportionate influence on his judgment, leading him to characterize a 94% success rate as unacceptable and consider switching to a measurably worse alternative.
structure.formal_form: Agent gives disproportionate weight to negative events E- relative to positive events E+ of comparable or greater magnitude. Negative events are more memorable, more emotionally vivid, and more influential on decisions than an equivalent number or magnitude of positive events.
structure.why_wrong: Three failures out of fifty contracts is a 6% failure rate. Replacing the Dustwalkers with the next-best option (81% reliability) would mean roughly ten failures per fifty contracts instead of three. Venn's emotional response to the negative events is leading him toward a decision that will produce more of exactly the outcomes he wants to avoid.
structure.counterpoint: Negativity bias has evolutionary roots — threats deserve more attention than routine safety. In some contexts, a single failure can be catastrophic enough to outweigh many successes (e.g., a bridge engineer). The bias becomes a problem when the negative events are not catastrophic but are treated as if they are, or when the comparison to alternatives is ignored.

assessment.identification_prompt: Venn says 'the bad ones stick with you.' He's right that the failures were real problems. But is he making a good decision by dropping the Dustwalkers? What is he not accounting for?

rubric.description: Player agrees with Venn that three failures are unacceptable and the Dustwalkers should be dropped.
Player senses Venn might be overreacting but cannot articulate why the failures feel so much bigger than the successes.
Player recognizes the 94% success rate is strong but does not explain why Venn is weighting the negatives so heavily or what the consequence of switching would be.
Player identifies negativity bias: the three failures loom larger in Venn's memory and emotional response than the forty-seven successes, and switching to a worse provider would increase failures.

Player identifies negativity bias, explains the asymmetry in how negative and positive events are weighted in memory and decision-making, calculates or estimates the comparative failure rates, and can articulate when heightened sensitivity to negatives is appropriate versus when it distorts judgment.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Venn wants to switch to the Ironwheel Guild at eighty-one percent reliability. Out of fifty contracts, how many failures would that be? Is that more or fewer than three? What does that tell you about whether switching actually solves Venn's problem?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Now consider: Venn says 'the bad ones stick with you.' He's describing how his own memory works. If you know your brain overweights negatives, what systems or practices could you put in place to counteract that when making business decisions?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Venn is a shrewd, experienced merchant who prides himself on high standards. He is not emotional in general, which makes his negativity bias harder to spot — it presents as rigorous quality control rather than irrational fear. Maren is his long-suffering trade secretary who keeps the actual numbers and quietly despairs when he ignores them.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Venn slides the contract across the table toward you. 'You're a traveller — you've used caravan companies. Would you trust a company that lost your cargo three times? I don't care what the numbers say. I remember what went wrong.'
game_hooks.resolution_path: If the player identifies the negativity bias, Maren produces a comparative ledger showing the Dustwalkers against every other company. The numbers are unambiguous. Venn, confronted with the data in context, grudgingly renews the contract but adds penalty clauses for future failures. He tells the player: 'You're right, and I hate it. The ones that go wrong just feel bigger.' He offers the player a merchant's discount at Thornport shops.

scenario.context: The crew of the brigantine *Sea Raven* has just weathered a fierce storm. Captain Marrick is reviewing the ship's recent performance before deciding whether to keep the veteran navigator, Silas, who has guided them through most voyages without incident.
scenario.text:
"Silas, you let the cargo of rum spill into the galley during the last squall," Captain Marrick growls, slamming his fist on the deck. "And two weeks ago you steered us onto the reef near Blackwater Cove—three men overboard! The worst of it was the night we lost the charted course and spent two days drifting. I can't trust a man who makes those mistakes. We're replacing you with a younger deckhand who swore he'll keep a steady hand on the wheel."

First Mate Lira steps forward, voice calm. "Captain, those three incidents are tragic, but out of the 42 voyages Silas has completed, 39 arrived at port on schedule and without loss. That's a 93% success rate, far better than any other navigator we've tried. The three mishaps are fresh in our minds because they cost us dearly, but the majority of voyages were flawless."
scenario.speaker_context: Captain Marrick is allowing three recent disasters to dominate his judgment, ignoring the overwhelming record of successful voyages. His decision to fire Silas would replace a 93% reliable navigator with an untested one, potentially lowering the ship's overall safety.

structure.pattern_description: Captain Marrick recalls the three recent failures vividly and gives them disproportionate weight, while the dozens of successful voyages have faded into the background. This emotional weighting leads him to deem the navigator unacceptable despite a high overall reliability rate.
structure.why_wrong: The captain is over‑valuing negative events and undervaluing the positive record, which can cause unnecessary crew turnover, loss of experience, and reduced mission success.
structure.counterpoint: First Mate Lira points out the statistical success rate, reminding the captain that isolated setbacks do not define overall performance.

assessment.identification_prompt: Which cognitive bias is Captain Marrick exhibiting when he focuses only on the three recent mishaps?

rubric.description: No answer or completely unrelated response.
Mentions a bias but cannot name it correctly.
Correctly identifies the bias as negativity bias.
Identifies the bias and explains how it influences the captain's decision.
Provides the correct identification, explanation, and suggests a concrete way to mitigate the bias (e.g., reviewing the full log of voyages).

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Explain why focusing only on the recent disasters is a bias and how looking at the full performance record would give a more balanced view.
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Great! Now think of a strategy the crew could use to keep the captain aware of the overall success rate during future decisions.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Captain Marrick is stern, quick‑to‑judge, and values reputation above all else.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: "Those three blunders still haunt me..."
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player can present the ship's logbook showing 39 successful voyages out of 42, or persuade another senior officer to vouch for Silas's reliability, leading the captain to reconsider his decision.

scenario.context: In the dusty courtyard of Blackrock Penitentiary, the yard supervisor, Officer Haines, asks the inmates to vote on whether to allow a new trade partnership with the "Scrap Yard Crew"—a group that supplies makeshift tools. The crew has a record of 92 successful trades out of 100, but three high‑profile incidents have caused serious injuries.
scenario.text: "Listen up," Officer Haines barked. "The Scrap Yard Crew says they're ready to supply us with new shivs and lock picks. They've delivered 92 out of 100 orders without a hitch. But three times they've sent broken blades that snapped during a fight, and once a batch of rusted locks caused a brawl that left two guys in the infirmary. That's four catastrophes. I don't trust them. We should go with the Iron Chain Syndicate, even though their success rate is only 78%." The crew's leader, Rook, clenches his fists. "Those four incidents stick in my mind. I can’t risk another broken shiv. The rest doesn't matter."
scenario.speaker_context: Rook’s fixation on the four negative incidents outweighs the ninety‑two successful deliveries, leading him to recommend a worse alternative despite better overall reliability.

structure.pattern_description: Rook (and Officer Haines) give disproportionate weight to a few negative events (broken tools, injuries) while ignoring the overwhelming majority of successful, safe trades. The vivid, painful memories of the failures dominate their judgment, causing them to reject a higher‑performing partner in favor of a less reliable one.
structure.why_wrong: The decision is based on an emotional over‑emphasis on rare negative outcomes rather than an objective assessment of overall success rates, leading to a sub‑optimal choice.
structure.counterpoint: If Rook were to consider the full record—92 successful trades versus 8 failures—he would see that the Scrap Yard Crew is statistically more reliable than the Iron Chain Syndicate, despite the painful memories of the few mishaps.

assessment.identification_prompt: What cognitive bias is Rook displaying when he dismisses the Scrap Yard Crew because of a few bad incidents, even though their overall success rate is higher?

rubric.description: No attempt to identify a bias.
Mentions the negative incidents but does not name the bias.
Identifies that a bias is present but mislabels it (e.g., "confirmation bias").
Correctly names the bias as "Negativity bias".
Correctly names the bias and explains how it skews Rook’s decision, referencing the disparity between the few negative events and the many positives.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Remember to think about how our minds sometimes give more weight to bad experiences than good ones. Which bias describes that tendency?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Well done! Recognizing negativity bias helps you see why Rook’s judgment is clouded. Use this insight to suggest a more balanced evaluation of the crew’s track record.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Rook is hardened, scarred by past betrayals, and tends to over‑react to any hint of danger.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: "I can still hear the snap of that broken shiv..."
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player can present the full trade statistics, propose a trial run with the Scrap Yard Crew, or mediate a discussion where the group weighs probability versus emotional memory, ultimately guiding Rook toward a decision based on data rather than fear.

scenario.context: The player gains access to the War Council of the city-state of Valdris, which is planning a pre-emptive strike on the neighbouring city of Korrath. The Council has been meeting in closed sessions for three weeks. Initially, several members had reservations, but by now the group has reached enthusiastic unanimous agreement. The player arrives as an outside advisor just before the final vote.
scenario.text: General Tova stands before a map bristling with pins. 'The plan is set. We strike at dawn in twelve days. Cavalry through the Ashford Gap, infantry along the river road, sappers through the old mine tunnels. Every member of this council has reviewed the plan and every member agrees: this is our moment.' She looks around the table. 'Does anyone wish to raise a final concern?' Silence. The player notices Lord Caelen shift uncomfortably in his seat but say nothing. After the session, the player catches Caelen in the corridor. He glances around nervously. 'You want the truth? The mine tunnels haven't been surveyed in eight years. We don't know if they're passable. I raised this in the second meeting and Tova said I was undermining morale. Councillor Drace told me that if I couldn't commit to the group, I should resign. After that... I stopped talking. We all stopped talking. Miren had concerns about the cavalry timing. She stopped too. Now everyone nods and smiles and says the plan is brilliant. It might be. But nobody has stress-tested it because nobody is allowed to ask hard questions anymore.'
scenario.speaker_context: The War Council has not reached genuine consensus through rigorous debate. Dissent was socially punished in early meetings, and members self-censored to maintain group harmony. The unanimity is an artifact of conformity pressure, not of the plan's actual soundness.

structure.pattern_description: The War Council exhibits classic groupthink: (1) the illusion of unanimity — silence is read as agreement; (2) direct pressure on dissenters — Caelen was accused of undermining morale and threatened with expulsion; (3) self-censorship — Caelen and Miren stopped raising concerns; (4) the illusion of invulnerability — 'this is our moment' suggests overconfidence. The result is a plan that has not been stress-tested because the social dynamics of the group prevent critical evaluation.
structure.formal_form: A cohesive group under directive leadership suppresses dissent through social pressure, self-censorship, and conformity norms, producing an illusion of unanimous agreement. The group's decision-making quality degrades because alternative viewpoints, risks, and counterarguments are never voiced or examined.
structure.why_wrong: The plan may have serious flaws (unsurveyed tunnels, questionable cavalry timing) that will only become apparent during execution, when the cost of failure is catastrophic. The council's unanimity does not reflect the actual distribution of opinions or concerns — it reflects the social cost of dissenting. A plan that cannot survive internal criticism is unlikely to survive contact with the enemy.
structure.counterpoint: Group cohesion is not inherently bad — military planning requires trust and commitment. The problem is when cohesion suppresses critical evaluation. Effective military councils historically used designated devil's advocates or red teams precisely to get the benefits of cohesion without the costs of groupthink.

assessment.identification_prompt: The War Council has reached unanimous agreement on the plan. General Tova seems confident that everyone is on board. But Lord Caelen tells you a different story. What is actually happening in this council, and why does unanimous agreement not mean the plan is sound?

rubric.description: Player takes the unanimity at face value and sees nothing wrong with the council's process.
Player recognizes that Caelen has been silenced but treats it as ordinary bullying or personality conflict rather than a systemic group dynamic.
Player identifies that dissent has been suppressed and the unanimity is false, but does not articulate the broader pattern or its consequences for decision quality.
Player identifies groupthink: social pressure and self-censorship have created an illusion of consensus, and the plan has not been critically evaluated because dissent is punished.

Player identifies groupthink, names multiple symptoms (illusion of unanimity, pressure on dissenters, self-censorship, illusion of invulnerability), explains how these degrade decision quality, and can propose structural remedies (devil's advocate, anonymous concern-raising, red-teaming the plan).

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: General Tova asked if anyone had concerns and nobody spoke. But Caelen told you he does have concerns — and so does Miren. If they have concerns but won't voice them, what does the silence actually tell you? Is it agreement or something else?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Here is the what-if: suppose you advise General Tova to appoint a devil's advocate — someone whose official job is to argue against the plan. Tova might say: 'That will weaken our resolve and waste time.' How would you respond? What is the cost of artificial dissent versus the cost of real but invisible doubt?

game_hooks.npc_personality: General Tova is a charismatic, decisive commander who values loyalty and unity. She is not a tyrant — she genuinely believes consensus means the plan is strong. She does not realize that she has created an environment where disagreement feels disloyal. Lord Caelen is thoughtful and courageous on the battlefield but conflict-averse in social settings. He knows the council is broken but fears the personal cost of saying so.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Caelen pulls you into an alcove and speaks barely above a whisper. 'Everyone in that room has doubts. I know because we used to talk freely at the first meetings. Then Tova shut me down and Drace threatened to have me removed. Now we all just nod. The plan might work — but nobody has tried to break it, and that terrifies me more than Korrath does.'
game_hooks.resolution_path: If the player identifies groupthink and proposes a structural solution (devil's advocate, anonymous written concerns, red team exercise), Caelen agrees to back the player in the next session. The player can present the concept to Tova, who initially resists but relents when Caelen and Miren finally voice their concerns. The red team exercise reveals the unsurveyed tunnels are partially collapsed, saving the plan from a fatal flaw. Tova, shaken, thanks the player and institutes a permanent red team for future war councils. The player gains Caelen and Miren as allies for future missions.

scenario.context: The player has just been assigned to the prison yard work detail. The yard’s informal leadership – the "Council of Ten" – is planning a coordinated protest against the guards. The council has met for three days, and by the final meeting everyone is nodding in agreement, despite early murmurs of doubt.
scenario.text: Captain Raze, the unofficial leader, slams his palm on the rusted metal fence. "Alright, brothers, the plan is simple. At the next headcount we’ll all step back from the fence, chant for fifteen minutes, then block the gate with the laundry carts. No one talks about it after this – we move as one. Any objections?" The yard falls silent. A younger inmate, Jax, shifts his weight, eyes flicking to the back wall, but says nothing. After the meeting, the player finds Jax leaning against the wall. "I tried to mention the laundry carts are rusty and could break under the weight," Jax whispers. "Raze called me a trouble‑maker, said I was hurting morale. The other guys laughed and told me to keep quiet. Now everyone’s just repeating the same script. No one’s checking if the carts can actually hold us. We’re all scared to speak up, so the plan stays untested."
scenario.speaker_context: The Council’s unanimity is not the result of thorough vetting but of social pressure. Dissenters were publicly chastised, leading the group to self‑censor, create an illusion of consensus, and ignore critical safety concerns.

structure.pattern_description: The inmates display classic groupthink: (1) Illusion of unanimity – silence is interpreted as agreement; (2) Direct pressure on dissent – Jax is labeled a trouble‑maker; (3) Self‑censorship – Jax and others stop voicing concerns; (4) Illusion of invulnerability – the plan is presented as flawless despite obvious risks; (5) Moral certainty – the protest is framed as the "right" thing, discouraging critique.
structure.why_wrong: The group’s decision is based on conformity, not on a critical assessment of the carts’ structural integrity. This can lead to a failed protest and possible injuries, illustrating how groupthink undermines sound decision‑making.
structure.counterpoint: Introduce a neutral third‑party (e.g., a senior guard or an external mediator) who encourages the inmates to list potential flaws, or have a character deliberately voice a contrary opinion without fear of retaliation to break the conformity pressure.

assessment.identification_prompt: Which cognitive bias is illustrated by the inmates’ refusal to question the protest plan?

rubric.description: No identification or incorrect bias named.
Names a bias but cannot explain why it applies.
Identifies Groupthink and mentions at least one characteristic (e.g., silence as agreement).
Identifies Groupthink and correctly links multiple characteristics from the scene (pressure on dissent, self‑censorship, illusion of unanimity).
Provides a thorough explanation, connects all five classic symptoms, and suggests how the bias could be mitigated in the scenario.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Explain that the silence in the yard is not genuine agreement but a result of pressure and self‑censorship, then ask the player to point out at least two specific actions that show this pressure.
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Praise the identification and ask the player to propose one concrete step the inmates could take to break the groupthink cycle.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Captain Raze is charismatic but authoritarian, thrives on unity and will quickly silence anyone who threatens the group's cohesion.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: "We move as one, or we lose everything. No doubts, no delays."
game_hooks.resolution_path: If the player helps Jax voice his concern safely (e.g., by rallying a small sub‑group or finding an ally among the guards), the protest plan is revised, the carts are inspected, and the yard avoids a potentially disastrous failure. Successful mitigation unlocks a 'Critical Thinking' badge.

scenario.context: The player, a junior defense attorney, has been invited to observe the deliberation chamber of the High Court of Valoria during the high‑profile murder trial of merchant Arlen Voss. The twelve jurors have been sequestered for three days. Early on, a few jurors voiced doubts about the key forensic evidence, but the foreperson, Juror Selene, repeatedly warned that “questioning the consensus will only give the prosecution more time to sway public opinion.” By the second day, the chamber has fallen into a tense quiet, with every juror nodding whenever the majority leans toward a guilty verdict. The player can choose to intervene by privately speaking with Juror Darrick, who looks uneasy.
scenario.text: Juror Selene stands, tapping the polished oak table. “We have reviewed the testimony, the blood spatter analysis, and the eyewitness accounts. The evidence points clearly to Mr. Voss. The majority has already indicated a guilty verdict. Does anyone have a reason to doubt this conclusion?” A heavy silence settles. The player notices Juror Darrick shift his weight, his eyes flicking to the window. After the session, the player catches Darrick in the hallway. He whispers, "I wanted to ask about the lab’s calibration logs, but Selene said anyone who ‘undermines the group’s confidence’ would be asked to leave. I’ve kept quiet because I don’t want to be the odd one out. The others keep nodding, and I’m afraid my doubt will be seen as betrayal."
scenario.speaker_context: The jurors have fallen into classic groupthink: an over‑confident foreperson pressures conformity, dissenters self‑censor, and the illusion of unanimity masks unresolved doubts about critical evidence.

structure.pattern_description: The jury exhibits classic groupthink: (1) Illusion of unanimity – silence is interpreted as agreement; (2) Direct pressure – the foreperson threatens social exclusion for dissent; (3) Self‑censorship – jurors hide doubts; (4) Mind‑guards – Selene dismisses challenges as harmful to morale; (5) Overconfidence – the group assumes the evidence is conclusive without rigorous re‑examination.
structure.why_wrong: The verdict may be based on unexamined flaws in forensic data and eyewitness reliability, leading to a possible miscarriage of justice. Groupthink suppresses critical analysis, increasing the risk of error.
structure.counterpoint: When might this heuristic be useful? In high‑stakes, time‑critical decisions where rapid consensus is needed, a tendency toward agreement can streamline action and prevent paralysis.

assessment.identification_prompt: After reading the scenario, identify which cognitive bias is driving the jurors' behavior and explain at least two specific indicators that reveal it.

rubric.description: Fails to name any bias or provides an unrelated bias; no supporting evidence.
Names a bias but not Groupthink; provides minimal or inaccurate evidence.
Correctly names Groupthink but cites only one indicator (e.g., silence as agreement).
Correctly names Groupthink and cites two distinct indicators (e.g., pressure from foreperson and self‑censorship).
Fully identifies Groupthink, cites multiple indicators (illusion of unanimity, direct pressure, self‑censorship, mind‑guarding), and explains why these undermine the trial's integrity.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: The NPC mentor, Senior Attorney Liora, says: “Notice how the foreperson frames any doubt as betrayal. When a group silences its own concerns, the decision quality drops. Look for the social pressures, not just the content of the discussion.”
assessment.follow_up_if_right: The mentor nods approvingly: “Exactly. Recognizing groupthink lets you ask the right questions and protect your client from a rushed, unchecked verdict.”

game_hooks.npc_personality: Juror Selene is charismatic, authoritative, and values harmony over conflict; Juror Darrick is conscientious, nervous, and fears ostracism.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Selene: “We cannot afford doubt now; the public is watching.” Darrick (whispering): “I’m uneasy about the lab reports, but…”.
game_hooks.resolution_path: If the player persuades Darrick to voice his concern publicly, the jury reopens discussion, allowing a forensic expert to testify about calibration errors, potentially shifting the verdict. If the player stays silent, the jury proceeds to a unanimous guilty verdict, and the bias remains unchecked.

scenario.context: The player visits a healer's hut in the forest village of Fernhallow. The healer, Old Sage Mirren, gives patients a special tonic for pain relief. She mixes it from ordinary herbs with no known medicinal properties, but her patients consistently report feeling better. A travelling physician, Doctor Alden, has arrived and is disturbed.
scenario.text: Doctor Alden confronts Mirren. 'I tested your tonic. It's chamomile water with honey. There is no active ingredient. You're deceiving your patients.' Mirren shakes her head calmly. 'I'm not deceiving anyone. I tell them it's a healing tonic, and they feel better. Every single one of them. You can test their grip strength, their sleep, their appetite — they improve. Are you going to tell a mother whose child sleeps through the night for the first time in weeks that she wasn't really helped?' Alden hesitates. 'But the tonic does nothing.' Mirren replies: 'The tonic does nothing. The belief does something. Are those the same?'
scenario.speaker_context: Mirren is demonstrating the placebo effect: the patient's belief that a treatment works can produce real, measurable physiological changes. Alden is committed to evidence-based medicine but is struggling with the fact that the placebo is genuinely helping people.

structure.pattern_description: The placebo effect occurs when a patient experiences real improvement due to their expectation of benefit, not due to any active treatment. It is 'dual' because it is both a genuine phenomenon (belief produces real effects) and a potential source of error (it can mask whether a treatment has any pharmacological value). Mirren's patients improve, but the improvement is caused by belief, not by the tonic. This is why controlled trials use placebos: to separate the effect of belief from the effect of the treatment.
structure.formal_form: Patient P receives treatment T with no active mechanism. P believes T is effective. P's condition improves. The improvement is caused by P's belief/expectation, not by T's pharmacological properties.
structure.why_wrong: The placebo effect can lead to false conclusions about treatment efficacy. If Mirren never tests against a control group, she cannot distinguish her tonic's effect from belief's effect. This is how ineffective treatments persist.
structure.why_right: The placebo effect is a real phenomenon with measurable physiological effects (pain reduction, immune modulation, stress response). It demonstrates the power of expectation and belief in shaping physical outcomes. Understanding it is essential for both medicine and epistemology.
structure.counterpoint: The ethical question is genuine: if the placebo helps and has no side effects, is it wrong to use it? Medical ethics generally says informed consent requires honesty, but the placebo only works if the patient believes. This creates a genuine dilemma, not a simple answer.

assessment.identification_prompt: Mirren's tonic has no active ingredients, yet her patients genuinely improve. Doctor Alden says the tonic does nothing. Who is right, and what is actually causing the improvement?

rubric.description: Player agrees with Alden that the patients are being deceived and cannot actually be improving, or agrees with Mirren that the tonic must work.
Player recognizes the patients feel better but attributes it to general comfort or attention rather than identifying the placebo mechanism.
Player identifies the placebo effect but treats it as purely psychological ('it's all in their heads') without recognizing the real physiological changes.
Player identifies the placebo effect, explains that belief/expectation produces real effects, and understands why controlled trials use placebos.

Player identifies the placebo effect as a real phenomenon, explains the epistemological problem (how do we know if a treatment works beyond placebo?), and engages with the ethical dilemma of using known placebos.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: The patients really do feel better — this is not about lying or imagination. Their pain decreases, their sleep improves. But the tonic is just chamomile water. If the tonic is not causing the improvement, what is?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Here is the harder question: if Mirren tells her patients the tonic is just chamomile water, will it still work? Recent research suggests that even 'open-label' placebos (where patients know it's a placebo) can produce effects. What does that tell you about the mechanism?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Mirren is calm, wise, and unapologetic. She has been healing for forty years and cares more about outcomes than mechanisms. Alden is rigorous, earnest, and genuinely conflicted — he cannot dismiss the results but cannot endorse the method.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Mirren pours a cup of tonic and slides it across the table. 'Drink it. I'm not going to tell you what it does. I'm going to let your body decide.'
game_hooks.resolution_path: If the player identifies the placebo effect and engages with the ethical dimension, both Mirren and Alden recognize them as a thoughtful interlocutor. Alden proposes a controlled trial: half the village gets Mirren's tonic, half gets plain water, neither group knows which. Mirren agrees, curious about the results. The player helps design the trial, unlocking a quest about experimental methodology.

scenario.context: During a tense jury deliberation in the stone hall of Greyhaven, the player, a junior counsel, notices that Elder Mara, a respected but anxious juror, is trembling as she pores over the testimony. Another juror offers her a cup of "calming draught" – a simple herbal tea that the town believes steadies the mind.
scenario.text:
Mara: "I don't know how to think straight after hearing that witness's scream. I feel my head spinning."

Jorik (the offering juror): "Here, take this tea. It's been used for generations to calm nerves before making hard choices. I swear it works."

*The player may give the tea to Mara or decline.*

Mara (after sipping): "Ah, I feel steadier now. The facts seem clearer. I think the defendant's guilt is obvious."

Judge Corwin (offstage, via intercom): "Remember, jurors, you must base your verdict on evidence, not on feelings."

Mara: "I know, but I trust my mind is sharper now. I will vote to convict."
scenario.speaker_context: Elder Mara is showing the placebo effect: her belief that the herbal tea will calm her leads her to feel more confident and to interpret the evidence in a way that aligns with her heightened certainty, even though the tea has no pharmacological impact.

structure.pattern_description: A person experiences real changes—often reduced anxiety or increased confidence—simply because they believe a treatment works, even when the treatment contains no active ingredients. In a jury setting, this can cause a juror to feel mentally 'clearer' and lean toward a verdict based on that false sense of clarity rather than the evidence alone.
structure.formal_form: Juror J receives inert treatment T. J believes T is effective. J's subjective state improves (e.g., confidence, calm). J's judgment about evidence changes because of the altered state, not because T altered the evidence.
structure.why_wrong: Relying on a placebo-induced confidence can mask the juror's true uncertainty, leading to a verdict that reflects perceived mental sharpness rather than an objective weighing of the facts. This may cause wrongful convictions or acquittals.
structure.why_right: The belief that a calming aid works can genuinely reduce stress, allowing a juror to process information without the interference of anxiety. In high‑stress deliberations, a modest reduction in nervousness can help jurors focus, provided they remain aware that the effect is psychological, not evidential.
structure.counterpoint: When might this heuristic be useful? In situations where a juror's anxiety is so high that it impairs comprehension, a harmless placebo can restore functional calm, enabling clearer deliberation—so long as the juror recognises the effect is psychological and does not let it substitute for evidence.

assessment.identification_prompt: Which cognitive bias is illustrated by Elder Mara's reliance on the herbal tea to feel more confident about the defendant's guilt?

rubric.description: Provides no answer or unrelated response.
Names a bias but not the placebo effect (e.g., "confirmation bias").
Identifies the placebo effect but gives only a minimal definition.
Correctly identifies the placebo effect and explains that the belief in the tea altered Mara’s confidence, affecting her verdict.
Fully articulates the dual nature: the tea genuinely reduced anxiety (value) yet created a false sense of certainty that could mislead the jury (limitation), linking both to the scenario.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Hint: The juror’s change in confidence comes from believing the tea works, not from any magical property of the tea itself. Think about how expectations can shape perception.
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Excellent! You spotted the placebo effect and its double‑edged impact on jury deliberations. Understanding this helps you spot when confidence is based on belief rather than evidence.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Elder Mara is wise and respected but highly superstitious; she trusts traditional remedies and fears making the wrong decision.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed:
"I feel the weight of this verdict on my shoulders. A little calm would help me think straight..." "This tea has steadied my mind; the facts now speak louder."
"I know we must rely on evidence, but my heart is steadier now."
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player can (1) give Mara the tea, (2) refuse to give it, or (3) suggest a short meditation instead. Each choice leads to a different deliberation outcome and a short reflection on whether the juror’s confidence is evidence‑based.

scenario.context: The player arrives at the bustling Admissions Hall of Ardentspire University during the annual Open Campus Day. Among the crowd, a charismatic senior named Maya runs a small table covered with glittering trinkets and a handwritten sign that reads, "Focus Amulet – Boost Your Interview Confidence!" Maya hands a polished stone amulet to each prospective student, claiming it helped her secure a spot in the competitive Honors Program.
scenario.text:
"Take this, it's the little stone that got me through my interview," Maya says, slipping the amulet into the player's hand. "I still remember the day I wore it—my nerves vanished, and I answered every question clearly. It doesn't change your GPA or SAT scores, but it sure changes how you feel when you walk into the room. Trust it, and you'll walk in with confidence."

The player can ask Maya how the amulet works, point out that it has no magical properties, or suggest alternative preparation methods. Maya smiles knowingly, "The stone itself does nothing, but believing it does is what makes the difference. Your mind decides whether you’re nervous or poised. That's the real power."

Behind Maya, a stern Admissions Officer watches, skeptical of the ritual but curious about the students' calm demeanor.
scenario.speaker_context: Maya is unintentionally demonstrating the placebo effect: the belief that the amulet will improve performance reduces anxiety and leads to better interview behavior, even though the amulet has no intrinsic effect on the student's qualifications.

structure.pattern_description: The placebo effect occurs when a person's expectation of benefit from a treatment (or object) leads to real, measurable improvements in mind‑influenced outcomes, despite the treatment having no active properties. It is 'dual' because the belief can produce genuine short‑term gains (e.g., reduced anxiety, better focus) while simultaneously masking the fact that the underlying skill or metric (e.g., test scores, GPA) remains unchanged.
structure.formal_form: If Person P receives inert object O and believes O will improve outcome X, then P's perception of X improves (e.g., lower anxiety, higher confidence). The actual value of X (objective measure) remains unchanged.
structure.why_wrong: Relying on a placebo can give a false sense of security, leading students to neglect concrete preparation (studying, practicing essays) that actually affects admissions criteria. It may also cause admissions staff to misattribute success to the amulet rather than to the student's own abilities.
structure.why_right: The belief‑driven boost can reduce performance‑killing stress, allowing a student to showcase existing abilities more effectively during interviews or presentations. Understanding this effect helps educators harness confidence‑building techniques without misleading students about causality.
structure.counterpoint: When might this heuristic be useful? The placebo effect can be ethically employed to improve morale or reduce anxiety, provided it is transparent and does not replace necessary skill development.

assessment.identification_prompt: After speaking with Maya, which of the following best describes the cognitive bias she is displaying?

rubric.description: Does not recognize any bias; provides unrelated answer.
Mentions that Maya's amulet is a belief but does not connect it to performance effects.
Identifies that Maya's belief influences confidence, hinting at placebo, but misses the dual nature.
Correctly names the placebo effect and explains both the beneficial confidence boost and the limitation that it does not improve objective scores.
Accurately names the placebo effect, explains its dual nature, and proposes an appropriate response (e.g., combine confidence aids with real study preparation).

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Maya chuckles, "Sometimes belief is all we have, but maybe a little extra practice wouldn't hurt either," and offers the player a study guide.
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Maya nods appreciatively, "Exactly. The stone helps the mind, but the mind still needs the knowledge. Good luck, scholar!" She then gives the player a bonus to their next confidence check.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Enthusiastic, slightly mystical, genuinely wants to help students feel confident, but unaware that her advice leans on superstition.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Believe in the stone, and the stone believes in you. Confidence is the real magic here. I never studied the interview questions, but I never felt the fear.
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player can (a) accept the amulet, gaining a temporary +2 confidence boost for the upcoming interview mock (but no change to objective stats), (b) decline and instead receive a detailed interview prep booklet, granting a permanent +1 to interview skill, or (c) suggest a blend of both, earning a small reputation bonus with the Admissions Officer for balanced advice.

scenario.context: The player visits a military outpost where Commander Voss has issued a mandatory order: all soldiers must attend a training drill on battlefield medicine. The order is reasonable — medics are scarce and basic wound care saves lives. But several soldiers are now refusing to attend, specifically because it was made mandatory.
scenario.text: Sergeant Kael leans against the barracks wall. 'I actually wanted to learn field medicine. Signed up for the optional course last month. Then Voss made it mandatory — attend or face disciplinary action. Now? I don't want to go. I know that makes no sense. The content is the same. The training is useful. But the moment someone tells me I have to do something, something in me wants to do the opposite.' He shakes his head. 'Three other soldiers feel the same way. Doss was already halfway through the manual — now he won't touch it. It's like Voss made the training worse by making it required.'
scenario.speaker_context: Sergeant Kael is self-aware enough to recognize that his reaction is irrational. He wanted to attend before the mandate and the training itself has not changed. His resistance is a response to the loss of autonomy, not to the content of the training.

structure.pattern_description: Reactance is a motivational response to perceived threats to personal freedom. When people feel their autonomy is restricted — even by a reasonable mandate — they experience an urge to restore their freedom by doing the opposite of what is required. Kael wanted the training when it was optional but resists it now that it is mandatory. The content, value, and timing are identical; only the framing (optional vs. required) changed. His resistance is not about the training but about the loss of choice.
structure.formal_form: Agent A freely chooses to do X. Authority B mandates X. A's motivation to do X decreases or reverses, not because X changed but because A's perceived freedom to choose X was eliminated.
structure.why_wrong: Reactance causes people to act against their own interests solely to reassert autonomy. Kael would benefit from the training and wanted it before the mandate. His refusal serves no purpose except restoring a feeling of freedom, at the cost of a skill that could save his life.
structure.counterpoint: Reactance is not always irrational. Sometimes mandates signal that an authority is overreaching, and resistance is a healthy check on power. The error occurs when reactance operates automatically, overriding the person's own prior assessment of the activity's value.

assessment.identification_prompt: Kael wanted to learn field medicine when it was optional. Now that it's mandatory, he doesn't want to go. The training itself hasn't changed. What is driving his resistance?

rubric.description: Player agrees with Kael that mandatory training is inherently worse and his resistance is justified.
Player sees Kael's reaction as stubbornness but cannot identify the underlying mechanism.
Player recognizes that the change from optional to mandatory is the trigger but does not name reactance or explain the autonomy mechanism.
Player identifies reactance: the resistance is a response to perceived loss of freedom, not to any change in the training's value.
Player identifies reactance, explains the autonomy mechanism, recognizes Kael's self-awareness as unusual, and can distinguish healthy resistance to overreach from irrational reactance.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Nothing about the training changed — same instructor, same content, same schedule. The only thing that changed was whether Kael chose to attend. If the content is the same, what made him not want it?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Now consider Commander Voss's dilemma: the training really is important and some soldiers were not going to attend voluntarily. How do you make essential training happen without triggering reactance? Is there a way to preserve the feeling of choice within a requirement?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Kael is honest, self-reflective, and slightly embarrassed by his own reaction. He knows it is irrational but cannot shake it. He is the rare NPC who diagnoses his own bias halfway but cannot overcome it alone.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Kael holds up the field medicine manual. 'I was reading this for fun last week. Now I can't open it without feeling like someone is forcing my hand. Tell me that's not ridiculous.'
game_hooks.resolution_path: If the player identifies reactance, Kael agrees to attend but asks the player to help Commander Voss reframe future mandates in ways that preserve perceived autonomy (e.g., choice of session time, optional advanced modules). Voss is initially resistant but agrees to a trial. Attendance and engagement both improve. The player earns a military advisor credential.

scenario.context: The player, a charismatic adventurer, is in the bustling marketplace of Valoria. They have been chatting with Liora, a charismatic bard who has hinted she might enjoy a sunset picnic by the river. The player decides to propose a surprise date to impress her.
scenario.text:
Liora leans against the spice stall, eyes sparkling. "You know, I love the idea of a quiet picnic by the river. It's been on my mind lately."

You smile and say, "How about I plan a surprise picnic for us tonight? I’ll bring the wine and a blanket."

Liora's expression shifts. "I appreciate the thought, but I don’t think I’ll go. I feel like I should decide on my own, not have you decide for me. If you set it up, it just feels... forced. I’d rather stay here and enjoy the market."
scenario.speaker_context: Liora genuinely enjoys picnics and had expressed interest earlier, but the moment the player imposes a plan, she reacts by rejecting it, not because the picnic is undesirable, but because her sense of autonomy feels threatened.

structure.pattern_description: Reactance occurs when a person perceives their freedom to choose is being threatened, prompting them to resist or do the opposite of what is suggested, even if the suggestion aligns with their own preferences. Liora wanted a picnic, yet when the player tries to arrange it, she refuses simply to reassert her freedom.
structure.formal_form: Agent A desires outcome X. Agent B mandates or strongly suggests X, removing A's choice. A experiences motivational arousal to restore autonomy, leading to a rejection of X despite its intrinsic value.
structure.why_wrong: Liora’s refusal undermines her own enjoyment and the potential for a pleasant shared experience. The resistance is driven by a perceived loss of control rather than any real drawback of the picnic, causing unnecessary conflict and missed opportunity.
structure.counterpoint: Reactance can be useful when external pressures are truly coercive or manipulative, prompting individuals to protect their autonomy. The bias becomes problematic when the perceived threat is minor or illusory, leading to irrational self‑sabotage.

assessment.identification_prompt: Which cognitive bias is most likely driving Liora's sudden refusal of the surprise picnic?

rubric.description: No response or unrelated answer; does not identify any bias.
Mentions a bias but selects the wrong one (e.g., confirmation bias).
Identifies reactance but does not explain why it applies to Liora's behavior.
Correctly identifies reactance and provides a brief justification linking Liora's loss of perceived freedom to her refusal.
Fully articulates reactance, explains the subtle cue (player's prescriptive suggestion), and notes how the bias could be mitigated in future interactions.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Explain that Liora's refusal stems from feeling her freedom to choose a date was taken away, which is a classic sign of reactance. Discuss how offering her the option to plan instead can reduce this effect.
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Great! Recognizing reactance helps you adapt your approach—ask Liora what she’d like to plan herself, preserving her sense of autonomy while still creating a memorable experience.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Flirtatious, adventurous, values personal freedom above all; enjoys romance but resents feeling controlled.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: I love the idea, but I need to choose it myself. If you decide for me, I feel trapped, even if it sounds fun. Maybe we can plan it together? I want it to feel like my choice.

scenario.context: The player arrives in the quiet suburb of Willow Creek, where a new neighborhood curfew on loud music after 10 p.m. has just been enacted by the homeowners' association (HOA). The rule is meant to reduce complaints, and most residents agree it’s reasonable. However, some long‑time residents are now actively opposing the curfew, not because they dislike quiet evenings, but because the HOA made the rule mandatory.
scenario.text: Mrs. Alvarez leans on the fence of her front garden, arms crossed. "You know, I used to love playing my violin in the evenings. The kids in the street liked it, and I even organized a little weekly concert for the kids. Then the HOA board announced the curfew and said, ‘From now on, no music louder than 30 dB after ten.’ Suddenly I feel like I can’t play at all. I don’t want to go to the next HOA meeting to discuss it. The rule itself isn’t the problem—quiet evenings are fine—but because they told us we have to follow it, I just want to ignore it. I’m even thinking of playing louder tomorrow just to prove they can’t control me."
scenario.speaker_context: Mrs. Alvarez is a long‑standing, music‑loving resident who previously welcomed community events. Her resistance is triggered by the perception that her personal freedom to choose when to play music has been taken away, even though the curfew is reasonable and benefits the neighborhood.

structure.pattern_description: Reactance is a motivational response to perceived threats to personal freedom. When an authority imposes a rule, even a reasonable one, the individual may feel compelled to do the opposite to restore autonomy. Mrs. Alvarez wanted to play music before the curfew was mandated; the rule itself hasn't changed the value of music, but the loss of choice makes her want to defy it.
structure.why_wrong: Her opposition harms both herself and the community: she forgoes a cherished activity and risks penalties, while the neighborhood loses a cultural contribution. The resistance is driven solely by a need to reassert autonomy, not by any real flaw in the curfew.
structure.counterpoint: Reactance can serve as a useful check when rules are overreaching or unjust. In this case, the curfew is reasonable, so the bias leads to an irrational overreaction rather than a healthy critique.

assessment.identification_prompt: Which cognitive bias is Mrs. Alvarez displaying when she says she wants to play louder just because the HOA made the curfew mandatory?

rubric.description: Does not recognize any bias or confuses it with unrelated concepts.
Mentions a bias but selects the wrong one (e.g., conformity, authority bias).
Identifies reactance but provides an incomplete or partially inaccurate explanation.
Correctly names reactance and explains that the resistance stems from perceived loss of freedom rather than the rule’s content.
Fully articulates reactance, cites the formal pattern, and notes why the bias is detrimental in this context.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Explain that Mrs. Alvarez’s urge to defy the curfew is not about the rule’s fairness but about feeling forced. Ask the player to think of a time they resisted something simply because it was mandated, and how that felt.
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Praise the player for spotting reactance. Offer a tip: when you notice this feeling, pause and evaluate whether the underlying action is actually beneficial before acting oppositely.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Warm, community‑oriented, slightly stubborn, values personal expression and has a strong sense of independence.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Mrs. Alvarez expresses love for music, mentions past community concerts, then shifts to frustration about the curfew being imposed, culminating in a threat to play louder as a protest.
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player can (a) persuade her to attend the HOA meeting by framing it as a choice to influence the rule, (b) suggest a compromise like a designated music hour, or (c) respect her decision and note the bias for later reflection.

scenario.context: The player meets a young bard named Finch backstage at a tavern performance. Finch played a beautiful set but stumbled over the opening chord of one song. He is now convinced his reputation is destroyed and refuses to perform again.
scenario.text: Finch sits with his lute across his knees, head in his hands. 'Did you hear that? The opening of Maiden's Lament — I hit a wrong note. The whole tavern heard it. Everyone is talking about it. I could feel them staring.' The player glances at the tavern — the audience is laughing, drinking, and discussing the evening's gossip. The barkeep says, 'Great show tonight. Best we've had in weeks.' A patron adds, 'Loved the ballad about the sea captain. What was that called?' Nobody mentions the wrong note. Nobody appears to have noticed.
scenario.speaker_context: Finch is experiencing the spotlight effect: the belief that others are paying far more attention to his mistakes than they actually are. He is the center of his own experience and projects that centrality onto everyone else.

structure.pattern_description: The spotlight effect is the tendency to overestimate how much other people notice and remember our appearance, behavior, and mistakes. Finch assumes the entire tavern registered his wrong note because it was vivid and distressing to him. In reality, most audience members were only loosely attending, filtered the error through their overall positive experience, or simply did not notice. People are far less attentive to us than we believe because they are preoccupied with their own concerns.
structure.formal_form: Agent A experiences salient event E (a mistake). A estimates P(others noticed E) >> actual P(others noticed E). A's estimate is anchored to the salience of E in A's own experience, not to others' actual attention.
structure.why_wrong: The spotlight effect can cause social avoidance, anxiety, and missed opportunities. Finch's one wrong note is trivial in the context of a full performance, but his overestimation of others' attention is enough to make him quit performing entirely.
structure.counterpoint: Sometimes people really are paying attention, especially if the mistake is severe or the stakes are high. A diplomat's gaffe or a surgeon's error is not a spotlight effect — it is genuine scrutiny. The bias applies specifically when we overestimate routine attention in low-stakes situations.

assessment.identification_prompt: Finch is convinced the audience noticed his wrong note and is judging him for it. The audience seems unaware. What cognitive error is Finch making, and why is his estimate of others' attention so far off?

rubric.description: Player agrees with Finch that the audience definitely noticed and his reputation is damaged.
Player thinks Finch is overreacting but attributes it to anxiety rather than a cognitive bias.
Player recognizes that the audience probably did not notice but cannot explain why Finch's estimate is systematically wrong.
Player identifies the spotlight effect: Finch overestimates how much others noticed because the mistake is salient to him, not because it is salient to them.
Player identifies the spotlight effect, explains the egocentric projection mechanism, and can distinguish situations where the bias applies from situations where scrutiny is genuinely high.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Think about the last time you were in an audience. How much do you remember about any performer's individual mistakes? Now think about the last mistake you made in front of others. Which one feels bigger?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Now consider: the spotlight effect might actually be adaptive in some contexts. If our ancestors assumed others were watching, they might have been more careful about social norms. When is overestimating attention useful, and when does it become paralyzing?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Finch is talented, sensitive, and prone to catastrophizing about social judgment. He is not fishing for compliments — he genuinely believes his career is over. He is endearing in his misery.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Finch peers at you through his fingers. 'You were out there. You heard it. Be honest — on a scale of one to complete disaster, how bad was it?' He braces for the worst.
game_hooks.resolution_path: If the player identifies the spotlight effect, they can walk Finch through the tavern, asking patrons what they remember. Nobody mentions the wrong note. Finch is stunned. He agrees to perform again, and the player earns a permanent bard companion who provides morale bonuses — and occasionally needs reassurance about his latest 'disaster.'

scenario.context: During the siege of Redwall Keep, the player encounters a young squire named Aldric on the battlements. Aldric's shield has a small crack that appeared when a stone struck it earlier in the day. He believes the enemy archers have spotted the flaw and are now targeting him specifically.
scenario.text:
"Sir! You saw that, didn't you? That crack in my shield—I'm sure the enemy can see it from miles away. They're laughing at me, waiting for the perfect shot. I can't stand the thought of them all focusing on my mistake!" Aldric grips the cracked shield tightly, eyes darting to the distant enemy walls. The veteran knight beside him chuckles, "The enemy cares more about the walls than a tiny fissure, lad. Keep your head up."
The player hears the clatter of swords, the thud of trebuchet stones, and the distant shouts of soldiers, but no one calls out Aldric's shield.
scenario.speaker_context: Aldric is experiencing the spotlight effect: he overestimates how much the enemy troops notice his cracked shield, believing it to be the center of their attention despite evidence to the contrary.

structure.pattern_description: The spotlight effect is the tendency to overestimate how much other people notice and remember our appearance, behavior, and mistakes. Aldric assumes the entire enemy force is fixated on his cracked shield because the flaw feels salient to him. In reality, the besieging army is preoccupied with the larger battle and likely does not notice a small imperfection on a single shield.
structure.formal_form: Agent A experiences salient event E (a personal flaw). A estimates P(others notice E) >> actual P(others notice E). A's estimate is anchored to the vividness of E in A's own perception, not to the actual attentional resources of others.
structure.why_wrong: The spotlight effect can lead to unnecessary anxiety, hesitation, and loss of confidence in high‑stakes situations like a siege. Aldric's belief that the enemy is targeting him because of a minor crack may cause him to act irrationally or abandon his post, jeopardizing the defense.
structure.counterpoint: While it's true that noticeable damage can attract attention, in large combat scenarios most combatants focus on strategic targets rather than individual imperfections unless they become a clear tactical advantage.

assessment.identification_prompt: Which cognitive bias is Aldric showing when he believes the enemy archers are all watching his cracked shield?

rubric.description: No answer or unrelated response; does not recognize any bias.
Mentions that Aldric is nervous but does not name a bias.
Names a bias (e.g., "overthinking") but does not correctly identify the spotlight effect or gives an inaccurate definition.
Correctly identifies the spotlight effect but provides only a minimal explanation.
Correctly identifies the spotlight effect and explains why Aldric's perception is biased, referencing how others are likely focused on the siege rather than his shield.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong:
The player receives a whispered hint from a nearby veteran: "In battle, most eyes are on the walls, not a single crack. Think about how much people really notice when they're busy fighting."
The player is then prompted to reconsider Aldric's belief.
assessment.follow_up_if_right: The veteran nods approvingly: "Exactly. Your insight will help Aldric keep his composure. Offer him some reassurance and a plan to stay focused on the larger fight."

game_hooks.npc_personality: Aldric is anxious, eager to prove himself, and overly self‑critical, yet he respects experienced warriors.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Did you see that? Everyone's laughing at my shield! I can't stand the thought they're all pointing at me... If I slip, the whole wall could fall because of me!
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player can choose to (1) reassure Aldric, emphasizing that the enemy's attention is on the gates; (2) demonstrate the insignificance of the crack by showing it to the player; (3) distract Aldric with a tactical task, shifting his focus from the perceived spotlight to active contribution.
