scenario.context: The player visits a border town where two guilds — the Ironworkers and the Woodworkers — compete for municipal contracts. The town council has received identical proposals from both guilds for building a new bridge. The player sits in on the council deliberation where the Ironworkers' representative, Forge Master Dunn, evaluates both proposals.
scenario.text: Forge Master Dunn reviews the two proposals. 'The Ironworkers' proposal uses proven techniques, shows attention to detail, and reflects years of expertise. A solid, trustworthy plan.' He picks up the Woodworkers' proposal. 'The Woodworkers' proposal is... adequate. It's technically similar, but I question whether they have the institutional discipline to execute on time. Their journeymen are less experienced, and frankly, I've heard their quality control is inconsistent.' The player looks at both proposals side by side. They are nearly identical — same timeline, same cost, same materials specifications, same safety margins. A neutral engineer from outside the town has certified both as equally sound.
scenario.speaker_context: Dunn is not deliberately lying. He genuinely perceives the Ironworkers' proposal as superior because he is an Ironworker. His evaluation of the Woodworkers' proposal is colored by in-group favoritism — he trusts, values, and charitably interprets 'his people' while scrutinizing and discounting the out-group.

structure.pattern_description: In-group bias is the tendency to favor members of one's own group — evaluating their work more charitably, trusting them more readily, and attributing positive qualities to them — while viewing out-group members with suspicion, scrutiny, and less charitable interpretation. Dunn reads the same quality of work differently depending on who produced it. He gives the Ironworkers the benefit of the doubt ('proven techniques') and denies it to the Woodworkers ('I question whether...').
structure.formal_form: Agent A belongs to group G. A evaluates work W1 (from G) and W2 (from not-G). W1 and W2 are objectively equivalent. A rates W1 higher than W2. The difference is attributable to group membership, not to any quality difference in the work.
structure.why_wrong: In-group bias distorts evaluation, allocation, and justice. It means the best proposal does not always win — the in-group proposal does. Over time, it concentrates resources and opportunities within favored groups and excludes others regardless of merit.
structure.counterpoint: Group loyalty is not always irrational. Trusting known collaborators with track records is reasonable. In-group bias becomes problematic when it operates automatically and overrides objective evaluation, especially in contexts that demand fairness (contracts, hiring, justice).

assessment.identification_prompt: Forge Master Dunn rated the Ironworkers' proposal higher, but an independent engineer certified both as equivalent. What is driving Dunn's different evaluations of identical work?

rubric.description: Player accepts Dunn's assessment and assumes the Ironworkers' proposal must genuinely be better.
Player suspects Dunn is biased but attributes it to corruption or self-interest rather than a cognitive pattern.
Player recognizes Dunn favors his own guild but does not articulate in-group bias as a systematic pattern.
Player identifies in-group bias: Dunn evaluates equivalent work differently based solely on group membership, applying charitable interpretation to his group and skepticism to the other.
Player identifies in-group bias, explains the double standard in evaluation, and can propose structural solutions (blind review, independent evaluation) that mitigate the bias.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Imagine the names were removed from both proposals and Dunn read them without knowing which guild wrote which. Would he still rate them differently? What does that tell you about what is driving his evaluation?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: In-group bias is nearly universal. It emerges even in minimal groups — people randomly assigned to 'Team Red' favor Team Red within minutes. If the bias is this deep, can it be eliminated, or can we only design systems that work around it?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Dunn is honest, hardworking, and genuinely unaware of his bias. He would be offended if accused of corruption because he sincerely believes the Ironworkers are better. The Woodworkers' leader, Artisan Sable, is frustrated but has no language for what is happening.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Dunn looks genuinely puzzled when challenged. 'I'm not playing favorites. I'm calling it as I see it. The Ironworkers' proposal just feels more solid. You can sense the craftsmanship.'
game_hooks.resolution_path: If the player identifies in-group bias, the council institutes blind proposal review: guild names are removed before evaluation. The next contract goes to the Woodworkers, and Dunn is shocked to learn he rated their (unnamed) proposal highest. He sits quietly for a long time, then says: 'I really thought I was being fair.' The player earns a role as an impartial evaluator for future contracts.

scenario.context: The player enters the bustling Hearthstone Tavern in the border town of Grayhaven. The tavern is owned by Marta, a stout dwarf who has run the establishment for decades and treats the regular mining crew from the Iron Hills as family. A traveling merchant caravan arrives, and the caravan leader, Selene, asks Marta to store a crate of exotic spices for a week. Marta's regulars, a group of Iron Hills miners, request a large barrel of ale to be set aside for their nightly shift.
scenario.text:
"Marta, could you keep this crate safe for us?" Selene asks, laying the sealed wooden box on the counter.
Marta glances at the crate, then at the miners' request. "Sure thing, Selene. It'll be fine in the back room," she says, but then turns to the miners, "And you lot, you get the barrel—right where you need it. No problem."
Later, the player notices that the back room where Selene's spices are stored is colder, less ventilated, and the spices are placed near a drafty door, while the miners' ale barrel sits in the warm, cozy corner near the hearth. Both parties paid the same storage fee, and the conditions are objectively identical except for Marta's placement choices.
scenario.speaker_context: Marta is not intentionally trying to sabotage the merchant; she simply feels a stronger loyalty to the miners—her long‑time patrons—than to the unfamiliar caravan. Her decisions reflect in‑group favoritism, giving the miners better conditions while neglecting the out‑group merchant.

structure.pattern_description: In‑group bias is the tendency to favor members of one's own group—granting them better treatment, more trust, and charitable interpretation—while treating out‑group members with less generosity or scrutiny. Marta's storage choices show a clear preference for her regular miners over the newcomer merchant, despite both requests being equivalent.
structure.formal_form: Agent A belongs to group G. A evaluates request R1 from G and request R2 from not‑G. R1 and R2 are objectively equivalent. A provides R1 with more favorable conditions than R2 solely because of group membership.
structure.why_wrong: Marta's bias leads to unfair treatment of the merchant, potentially damaging trade relations and harming the tavern's reputation. The bias is unrelated to any real difference in the value or risk of the stored goods, making the decision irrational and unjust.
structure.counterpoint: If Marta evaluated the storage requests purely on objective criteria—such as temperature control, proximity to the hearth, and fee paid—both parties would receive identical conditions, eliminating the bias.

assessment.identification_prompt: What cognitive bias is Marta displaying when she stores the miners' ale in the warm corner but places the merchant's spices near a drafty door?

rubric.description: No identification of bias; answer is unrelated or blank.
Names a bias (e.g., "favoritism") but does not link it to in‑group bias or explain why.
Correctly identifies the bias as in‑group bias but provides only a minimal explanation.
Identifies in‑group bias and explains how Marta's loyalty to the miners causes the unequal treatment.
Provides a thorough analysis, linking the bias to potential consequences for the tavern, and suggests how Marta could correct the behavior.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Explain that Marta is favoring her regular patrons over the outsider, which is a classic example of in‑group bias. Consider how treating both parties equally would improve fairness.
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Great! Now think about how you, as the player, could help Marta recognize this bias and encourage her to store both items under the same conditions.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Marta is proud, loyal, and warm to those she knows, but wary of strangers. She values long‑standing relationships above new opportunities.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Marta might say, "You miners are like family—I'll make sure you get the best spot. As for strangers, they'll manage on their own, I suppose..."
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player can present the neutral storage guidelines to Marta, point out the unequal conditions, or offer to rearrange the items themselves, prompting Marta to reflect on her bias and adopt a fairer policy.

scenario.context: On the distant mining colony of Helios-9, the Central Council must choose a crew to refurbish the primary ore‑processing tunnel after a recent collapse. Two teams submit identical plans: the Core Diggers, who have worked the deep shafts for decades, and the Surface Extractors, a newer crew specialized in shallow deposits. The player, acting as the Council's senior advisor, listens to the lead foreman of the Core Diggers, Jara Voss, as she evaluates both proposals.
scenario.text: Jara Voss leans over the holo‑blueprints. "Our Core Diggers' plan uses the proven mag‑field stabilizers we’ve refined over twenty cycles. The tolerances are tight, the crew knows every seam, and the safety protocols are second‑nature. It’s a solid, trustworthy approach." She flips the display to the Surface Extractors' submission. "The Surface Extractors' plan looks… adequate. It mirrors ours in every technical metric, but I’m not convinced they have the same grit for a deep‑shaft operation. Their crews are newer, and I’ve heard they cut corners on equipment checks." The player can see that both proposals list identical materials, timelines, costs, and have been independently certified by an external engineering audit as equally viable.
scenario.speaker_context: Jara genuinely believes the Core Diggers' proposal is superior because she belongs to that crew. Her assessment of the Surface Extractors' plan is clouded by in‑group favoritism—she grants the benefit of the doubt to her own team while scrutinizing the out‑group despite no objective differences.

structure.pattern_description: In‑group bias is the tendency to favor members of one's own group—evaluating their work more charitably, trusting them more readily, and attributing positive qualities to them—while viewing out‑group members with suspicion, scrutiny, and less charitable interpretation. In this scenario, Jara rates the Core Diggers' proposal higher than the Surface Extractors' despite identical objective merit.
structure.formal_form: Agent A belongs to group G. A evaluates work W1 (produced by G) and work W2 (produced by not‑G). W1 and W2 are objectively equivalent. A assigns a higher quality rating to W1 than to W2. The rating difference is attributable solely to group membership, not to any actual difference in the work.
structure.why_wrong: Jara's judgment is distorted by her affiliation with the Core Diggers. By giving undue weight to her own crew and discounting the equally competent Surface Extractors, she risks an inefficient allocation of resources, demoralizes the out‑group, and undermines the colony's principle of merit‑based decision‑making.
structure.counterpoint: A rational counterpoint would note that an independent audit shows the two plans are indistinguishable in safety and cost. Selecting a crew based on objective performance metrics rather than affiliation would maximize tunnel stability and maintain colony cohesion.

assessment.identification_prompt: Identify the cognitive bias displayed by Jara Voss when she evaluates the two refurbishment proposals.

rubric.description: No recognition of bias; the answer is unrelated or blank.
Mentions a bias but mislabels it (e.g., calls it "favoritism" without linking to in‑group bias).
Correctly identifies that a bias is present but provides an incomplete or vague explanation of why it is in‑group bias.
Accurately names In‑group bias and explains that Jara’s preference stems from her membership in the Core Diggers, contrasting it with the objective equivalence of the proposals.
Provides a thorough explanation, referencing the formal definition, the impact on decision‑making, and connects the bias to broader colony consequences.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Explain how personal affiliation can cloud objective assessment, then ask the player to rewrite Jara's evaluation using only the audited data, removing any group‑based language.
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Praise the identification and prompt the player to suggest a procedural safeguard the Council could implement to prevent in‑group bias in future contract awards.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Jara Voss is proud, loyal to the Core Diggers, and values tradition over novelty. She is confident in her crew's reputation but can be persuaded with hard data.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: “Our crew has braved the deepest shafts, so you can trust our plan… but I’m not sure the Surface team can handle the pressure.”
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player can present the external audit, request a joint review panel, or appeal to the Council's merit‑based charter. Successfully mitigating the bias unlocks a "Fair Decision" achievement and improves inter‑crew trust.

scenario.context: The player is attending a trial in the court of Ashenmoor. Two suspects are accused of the same crime — stealing grain from the town granary. The evidence against both is identical: each was seen near the granary at night, each had grain dust on their clothes, and each lacks a verifiable alibi. The judge, Magistrate Yorn, is about to render verdicts.
scenario.text: Magistrate Yorn addresses the court. 'First, the case against Ella. Ella is a respected schoolteacher, kind to children, and known for her volunteer work at the temple. The evidence is circumstantial at best. Grain dust? She walks past the granary every day. Near the granary at night? She often visits the temple after dark. I find the case unconvincing.' He turns to the second case. 'Now, Rusk. Rusk is a drifter who arrived in town two months ago. No family, no steady work, drinks at the tavern most nights. The same evidence — grain dust, near the granary, no alibi — paints a much clearer picture. I find Rusk guilty.' The court clerk whispers to you: 'The evidence is identical. But Yorn likes Ella and distrusts Rusk. Watch how he explained the same facts differently for each.'
scenario.speaker_context: Magistrate Yorn is exhibiting the halo effect: his positive impression of Ella (likeable, kind, community-minded) causes him to interpret ambiguous evidence charitably, while his negative impression of Rusk (outsider, drifter) causes him to interpret the same evidence as damning.

structure.pattern_description: The halo effect is the tendency for a positive impression of someone in one domain (personality, appearance, likability) to influence judgment of them in unrelated domains (guilt, competence, trustworthiness). Yorn likes Ella, so he interprets ambiguous evidence in her favor. He distrusts Rusk, so he interprets identical evidence against him. The evidence has not changed — the lens through which it is evaluated has.
structure.formal_form: Agent forms positive impression I+ of person P1. Agent forms negative impression I- of person P2. Identical evidence E is evaluated: E|I+ is interpreted charitably; E|I- is interpreted harshly. The evaluation is driven by I, not E.
structure.why_wrong: The halo effect undermines fair evaluation by allowing an overall impression to contaminate specific judgments. In a courtroom, it means likeable defendants are acquitted and unlikeable defendants are convicted on the same evidence. The same pattern distorts hiring, grading, reviews, and any context where a general impression affects specific assessments.
structure.counterpoint: First impressions are not always irrelevant. Character evidence can be legitimately probative in some contexts. The error is in letting a general feeling override careful evaluation of specific evidence, especially when the stakes are high and fairness demands equal treatment.

assessment.identification_prompt: Magistrate Yorn acquitted Ella and convicted Rusk on identical evidence. What is different between the two cases, and how is it affecting his judgment?

rubric.description: Player accepts the verdicts and believes the evidence must be different for each case or that character justifies the distinction.
Player notices the verdicts are inconsistent but attributes it to simple personal dislike rather than a cognitive pattern.
Player recognizes that Yorn likes Ella and dislikes Rusk, and that this is influencing his interpretation of the evidence, but does not name the halo effect.

Player identifies the halo effect: Yorn's positive impression of Ella causes charitable interpretation of evidence, while his negative impression of Rusk causes harsh interpretation of the same evidence.

Player identifies the halo effect, explains how it distorts evaluation of specific evidence, connects it to systemic injustice, and proposes structural safeguards (blind review of evidence, standardized evaluation criteria).

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Cover up the names and read just the evidence for each case. Grain dust. Near the granary. No alibi. Can you tell which suspect is which from the evidence alone? If not, why did Yorn reach different conclusions?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: The halo effect does not just operate in courtrooms. Think about job interviews, student evaluations, or product reviews. How does liking someone change how you evaluate their work? What structures can prevent this?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Magistrate Yorn is not corrupt — he is genuinely unaware that his liking for Ella and distrust of Rusk are coloring his evaluation. He considers himself scrupulously fair. The court clerk is observant and troubled but does not have the authority to intervene.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: The court clerk pulls you aside. 'Did you notice what just happened? Same evidence, opposite verdicts. I've seen Yorn do this before — the people he likes always seem to have weaker evidence against them. He doesn't see it.'
game_hooks.resolution_path: If the player identifies the halo effect, the court clerk asks them to present the argument to the appeals council. The player presents the evidence side by side, stripped of personal details. The council overturns Rusk's conviction and orders a fair retrial for both. Yorn is initially defensive but later acknowledges the pattern. The player earns a role as a court advisor.

scenario.context: It is the height of the harvest season in the village of Goldfield. The council must choose which of two laborers will oversee the loading of the final grain wagon that will travel to the neighboring town for trade. Both laborers have identical records: they each lifted the same amount of grain, both were seen near the storage barns at dusk, and neither has any documented mistake this season.
scenario.text: Elder Lady Maren steps forward. 'First, let us speak of Thom. Thom is the village's songbird; his morning chants lift everyone's spirits, and he always offers a fresh loaf to the orphanage. The grain dust on his sleeves? He merely walks the fields each day. Seeing him near the barns at night? He often checks the lanterns after his songs. I see no cause for concern.' She turns to the second laborer. 'Now, consider Jarek. Jarek arrived from the hills last spring, keeps to himself, and never joins the communal feasts. The same grain dust, the same night sightings—these point to a careless worker. I find Jarek unfit to lead the wagon.' A nearby farmer whispers, 'The facts are the same, but Lady Maren's opinion of Thom and Jarek colors her judgment.'
scenario.speaker_context: Lady Maren is exhibiting the halo effect: her positive feelings toward Thom's singing and generosity cause her to interpret ambiguous evidence in his favor, while her negative view of Jarek leads her to see the same evidence as incriminating.

structure.pattern_description: The halo effect occurs when a person's overall impression of someone (often based on likable traits) influences judgments about that person's unrelated qualities or actions. Here, Lady Maren's admiration for Thom's kindness leads her to downplay evidence, whereas her dislike of Jarek leads her to overstate the same evidence.
structure.why_wrong: Lady Maren lets unrelated personal feelings dictate a critical decision about competence. The identical evidence should be evaluated neutrally; letting a 'halo' of likability or distrust sway judgment creates an unfair outcome.
structure.counterpoint: The village elder, Brother Calen, points out that both laborers have the same record and asks the council to base the decision solely on the documented evidence, not on personal reputation.

assessment.identification_prompt: Which cognitive bias is Lady Maren displaying when she judges Thom and Jarek differently despite identical evidence?

rubric.description: No identification or incorrect bias named.
Names a bias but cannot explain why it applies.
Identifies the halo effect but gives an incomplete or partially inaccurate explanation.
Correctly identifies the halo effect and explains how Lady Maren's feelings influence her interpretation of the evidence.
Provides a thorough explanation, cites specific statements, and contrasts the bias with a correct, evidence‑based approach.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Explain that the halo effect is about letting a positive (or negative) impression of a person spill over into unrelated judgments. Show how Lady Maren's praise of Thom's singing leads her to excuse the grain dust, while her disdain for Jarek leads her to condemn him.
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Great! You spotted the halo effect. Use this insight to advise the council to base the wagon leadership decision on the identical performance records alone.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Elderly, benevolent, but prone to letting personal affection guide decisions.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: I trust those who bring joy to the fields, not those who keep to the shadows.
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player can either accept Lady Maren's decision, challenge her by presenting the neutral evidence to the council, or seek Brother Calen's counsel to re‑evaluate the choice without bias.

scenario.context: You have just been appointed assistant coordinator for the Brightheart Volunteer Guild in the town of Luminara. The guild is preparing two parallel projects for the upcoming Harvest Festival: a high‑profile fundraising gala and a behind‑the‑scenes inventory audit. Two senior volunteers, Tomas and Lina, have identical experience records: five years of service, both have led small teams, and both received the same performance rating last quarter.
scenario.text:
Mara, the charismatic head of the guild, approaches you with a smile. "Tomas is such a natural people‑person—everyone loves his stories and he always brightens the hall. I think he’d be perfect for the gala, you know, the face of the event. Lina, on the other hand, is very diligent and detail‑oriented, but she’s a bit shy. She’d do great with the inventory work. What do you think?" She leans in, eyes sparkling, and adds, "You’ll see how much smoother the gala runs when the crowd sees someone they already adore."

You notice that the guild’s leadership board has already pre‑filled the assignments in the planning spreadsheet, matching Mara’s suggestion, even though the objective criteria (experience, past performance, availability) are identical for both volunteers.
scenario.speaker_context: Mara is exhibiting the halo effect: her positive personal impression of Tomas (charismatic, liked) leads her to overvalue his suitability for the public‑facing gala, while her neutral/less‑favorable view of Lina causes her to undervalue Lina’s ability to handle the same level of responsibility, despite equal qualifications.

structure.pattern_description: A positive (or negative) overall impression of a person influences specific judgments about their abilities, character, or suitability in unrelated domains. Here, Mara’s likability bias toward Tomas causes her to assign him the high‑visibility role, while Lina is relegated to a less visible task despite identical credentials.
structure.formal_form: Agent forms impression I+ of person P1 and I- of person P2. Identical qualification set Q is evaluated: Q|I+ → favorable assignment A+, Q|I- → less favorable assignment A-. The assignment decision is driven by I, not Q.
structure.why_wrong: The halo effect distorts fair decision‑making by allowing irrelevant affective impressions to outweigh objective evidence. In volunteer settings, this can lead to underutilized talent, reduced morale, and inefficient allocation of resources.
structure.counterpoint: When might this heuristic be useful? In rapid, low‑stakes social judgments where detailed analysis is impossible, a positive first impression can serve as a shortcut to trust someone quickly.

assessment.identification_prompt: Which cognitive bias is Mara displaying when she pushes Tomas onto the gala role despite his qualifications being identical to Lina's?

rubric.description: No identification of bias; response unrelated to the scenario.
Mentions a bias but selects the wrong one (e.g., confirmation bias).
Identifies the halo effect but cannot explain why it applies.
Correctly names the halo effect and gives a basic explanation linking Mara's likability impression to her assignment choice.
Fully articulates the halo effect, explains the subtlety of the bias, and contrasts it with a rational, evidence‑based decision.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Mara’s suggestion is driven by how much she likes Tomas, not by their equal qualifications. This is the halo effect: a general positive impression spilling over into specific judgments. In volunteer work, always check the objective criteria before letting personal feelings decide assignments.
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly! Mara’s favoritism toward Tomas illustrates the halo effect. Recognizing it helps you keep assignments fair and ensures the guild uses each volunteer’s skills effectively.

You’ll see how much smoother the gala runs when the crowd sees someone they already adore.

scenario.context: The player is walking through a crowded market square in the city of Coppergate when they witness a pickpocket steal a merchant's purse in broad daylight. At least twenty people saw it happen. The merchant shouts for help. Nobody moves.
scenario.text: The merchant stumbles and shouts: 'Thief! He took my purse! Someone stop him!' The player looks around. Twenty people stand frozen. A baker watches from his stall. A guard leans against a wall, looking at the crowd, apparently waiting for someone else to act. A woman clutches her child and steps back. The thief jogs unhurriedly toward the alley, not even running. He knows no one will act. The baker mutters to his apprentice: 'Someone will get him.' The guard thinks: 'Not my patrol sector.' The woman thinks: 'Surely someone closer will help.' Nobody moves.
scenario.speaker_context: Every bystander has a reason not to act, and that reason is the same: the presence of other bystanders. Each person assumes someone else will intervene, and this assumption is shared by everyone, resulting in collective inaction.

structure.pattern_description: The bystander effect occurs when the presence of others reduces each individual's sense of personal responsibility to act. In a crowd, each person assumes someone else will intervene (diffusion of responsibility), looks to others' inaction as a signal that action is not needed (pluralistic ignorance), and fears embarrassment from acting in a situation others seem to deem non-urgent (evaluation apprehension). The result: the more witnesses, the less likely any single person is to help.
structure.formal_form: N bystanders witness emergency E. Each bystander i estimates P(someone else acts) as high because N is large. Each bystander i's probability of acting, P(i acts), decreases as N increases. If all reason identically, P(anyone acts) approaches zero as N grows.
structure.why_wrong: The bystander effect turns numbers — which should increase the chance of help — into a liability. Each additional witness reduces rather than increases the probability of intervention because responsibility is diffused across more people. The victim is worse off in a crowd than with a single witness.
structure.counterpoint: The bystander effect is not inevitable. Research shows that assigning specific responsibility ('You in the red shirt, call for help') breaks the diffusion. Training and cultural norms also mitigate the effect. The pattern describes a default, not an unbreakable law.

assessment.identification_prompt: Twenty people watched the theft and nobody acted. Each person had a reason — but it was the same reason. What is it, and why does having more witnesses make help less likely rather than more likely?

rubric.description: Player attributes the inaction to cowardice or apathy without identifying the structural mechanism.
Player recognizes people are waiting for someone else but does not explain why this paralysis increases with crowd size.
Player identifies diffusion of responsibility but does not connect it to pluralistic ignorance or evaluation apprehension.
Player identifies the bystander effect, explains diffusion of responsibility, and recognizes that each person's inaction reinforces the others'.

Player identifies the bystander effect with all three mechanisms (diffusion, pluralistic ignorance, evaluation apprehension), explains the paradox of crowd size, and can describe how to break the effect.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Imagine you were the only person in the square when the theft happened. Would you have acted? Now imagine twenty people around you, all standing still. Does their stillness change your impulse to help? Why?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Here is the practical lesson: if you ever need help in a crowd, do not shout 'someone help!' Instead, point to one specific person and say 'You, in the blue coat — call the guard.' Why does this work?

game_hooks.npc_personality: The baker is a decent person who genuinely assumed someone closer would act. The guard is bureaucratic and jurisdiction-minded. The thief is casual and experienced — he knows crowds are his best cover. The merchant is desperate and confused by the inaction.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: The merchant sits in the dirt, stunned. 'Twenty people. Twenty people watched. I looked right at the guard and he looked right back at me and did nothing. Is everyone in this city a coward?' The baker overhears and looks ashamed. 'I'm not a coward. I just thought... someone else...'
game_hooks.resolution_path: If the player identifies the bystander effect, the merchant asks how to prevent it in the future. The player helps establish a 'market watch' system where specific stall owners are assigned specific response roles, eliminating diffusion of responsibility. Theft in the market drops dramatically. The player earns the merchant's gratitude and a discount at all Coppergate shops.

scenario.context: The player attends the annual 'Moonlit Matchmaking' gathering in the bustling garden of the Silver Rose Inn. The event is designed for singles to mingle under lantern light, and dozens of hopeful daters are scattered among tables, chatting and sipping spiced wine.
scenario.text: At the far end of the garden, a nervous young woman named Lira fumbles her words as a charismatic suitor, Doren, publicly dismisses her with a scoff: "I don't have time for amateurs." Lira's cheeks flush, and she begins to retreat. Around them, ten other attendees watch. A flamboyant bard strums his lute, a group of merchants chat over their goblets, a pair of guards lean against a stone archway, and a shy scholar hides behind a flowerpot. None of them steps forward to comfort Lira or confront Doren. The player hears a whispered comment from a nearby merchant: "Someone will speak up eventually," while a guard thinks, "It's not my business; someone else will handle it." The scene freezes unless the player chooses to act.
scenario.speaker_context: Each bystander assumes someone else will intervene, so they remain passive. Their internal monologues reveal the diffusion of responsibility that keeps the situation static, allowing the emotional harm to continue unchecked.

structure.pattern_description: When multiple witnesses observe an uncomfortable or harmful social situation, each individual feels less personal responsibility to act, assuming others will intervene. This diffusion of responsibility leads to collective inaction, even when intervention could alleviate the victim's distress.
structure.why_wrong: The presence of many observers should increase the chance of help, but the bystander effect flips this expectation. Each person’s belief that someone else will step in reduces the overall likelihood that anyone will act, leaving the victim unsupported and potentially worsening the social harm.
structure.counterpoint: When a clear, individual responsibility is assigned (e.g., "You, the guard, please intervene"), the diffusion breaks down and people are more likely to act. Cultural norms that value chivalry or protective behavior can also mitigate the effect.

assessment.identification_prompt: After the scene, the game asks: "Why did the other attendees not step in to help Lira when Doren insulted her? Identify the cognitive bias at work."

rubric.description: No recognition of any bias; response unrelated to the scenario.
Mentions that people were hesitant, but cannot name the specific bias.
Identifies the general idea of "diffusion of responsibility" but does not label it as the bystander effect.
Correctly names the "Bystander effect" and explains that each person expected someone else to act.
Accurately names the Bystander effect, explains the underlying mechanisms (diffusion of responsibility, pluralistic ignorance), and links it to the specific NPC thoughts shown in the scene.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: A friendly mentor NPC appears and says, "Sometimes, when many people watch, everyone assumes someone else will step up. That's called the Bystander effect. Next time, try to look for that cue."
assessment.follow_up_if_right: The town's matchmaker nods approvingly: "Well spotted! Recognizing the Bystander effect lets you break the chain of inaction and become the hero of the night."

game_hooks.npc_personality: Lira is shy and earnest; Doren is boastful and dismissive; the bystanders range from indifferent merchant to overly confident guard, each displaying subtle self‑justifying thoughts.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Someone will step in, right?" mutters the merchant. It's not my job," the guard whispers to his companion. I don't want to make a scene," the scholar thinks, glancing at the lanterns.
game_hooks.resolution_path: If the player intervenes (e.g., offers comfort to Lira, confronts Doren, or calls a guard), the bystanders become startled and may follow the player's lead, turning the situation into a positive social moment. If the player ignores the scene, the bystanders remain passive, and Lira leaves the garden, reinforcing the bias.

scenario.context: The player is strolling through the tight alleys of the Willowbrook district after sundown. A lively block party is in full swing on the corner of Bramble Street, with music, lanterns, and a makeshift grill. Suddenly, a spark from the grill lands on a stack of wooden crates on the balcony of the adjoining apartment, igniting a small flame. Several residents and partygoers notice the flicker, but most keep their distance, chatting and drinking.
scenario.text: A teenage girl in a bright hoodie gasps, "Whoa, fire!" She glances toward the balcony, then back at the crowd. An elderly man leans on his cane, muttering, "Someone will call the watchmen." A neighbor holding a tray of food says, "It looks like the kids over there will put it out." A street performer pauses his lute, eyes the flames, then resumes playing, thinking, "Probably the landlord will handle it." The fire crackles louder, licking the wooden crates, but nobody steps forward. The player can either rush to the balcony to smother the flame, shout for help, or stay and observe.
scenario.speaker_context: Each bystander assumes another person will take responsibility for the emerging fire. Their internal dialogue reflects diffusion of responsibility and pluralistic ignorance, leading to collective inaction despite the obvious danger.

structure.pattern_description: When multiple observers are present, each individual feels less personal responsibility to act, assuming someone else will intervene. This diffusion of responsibility reduces the likelihood that any single person will intervene, even in urgent situations.
structure.why_wrong: The presence of many witnesses should increase the chance of help, but the bystander effect turns the crowd into a barrier: each person’s reluctance compounds, allowing a preventable hazard to grow. The fire could have been extinguished instantly if one person had acted, yet the collective hesitation lets it spread.
structure.counterpoint: The bystander effect can be useful when a situation is ambiguous or potentially dangerous to intervene in; waiting for clearer cues or an authority figure can prevent rash actions. In a chaotic battlefield, for example, it may be safer to let a trained guard handle an explosion.

assessment.identification_prompt: Which cognitive bias is most responsible for the crowd’s failure to act on the balcony fire?

rubric.description: Provides no answer or an unrelated concept (e.g., "magic" or "luck").
Names a bias but selects the wrong one (e.g., "confirmation bias").
Identifies the bystander effect but does not explain why it applies to the scenario.
Correctly identifies the bystander effect and briefly explains diffusion of responsibility in the scene.
Fully articulates the bystander effect, cites specific NPC thoughts that illustrate the bias, and connects it to the missed opportunity to stop the fire.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: The town elder steps in and says, "In crowds, people often wait for someone else to act. That's called the bystander effect. If you notice a danger, take the initiative or assign someone a clear task."
assessment.follow_up_if_right: A grateful neighbor nods, "Exactly. When everyone thinks someone else will help, nothing gets done. Your decision to act breaks that cycle."

game_hooks.npc_personality: The teenage girl is impulsive but hesitant; the elderly man is polite and deferential; the neighbor is laid‑back and relies on others; the street performer is proud and self‑absorbed.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Someone will call the watchmen... Looks like the kids will put it out... Probably the landlord will handle it... Whoa, fire!
game_hooks.resolution_path: If the player rushes to the balcony and extinguishes the flame, the NPCs comment on the player's decisive action and the crowd learns to assign responsibility. If the player does nothing, the fire spreads, causing property damage and a later quest to repair the neighborhood, highlighting the cost of inaction.

scenario.context: You are browsing stalls in Thornmarket Square. A dwarven gemcutter named Brecca waves you over. You need a fire opal for a crafting quest.
scenario.text: Brecca holds up a fire opal: 'This piece? Appraised at 900 gold by the Gemwright Guild themselves. But I can tell you've got an eye for quality. Tell you what — 600 gold, and it's yours today. You won't find a fairer deal in all of Thornmarket.' A merchant at the next stall overhears and mutters: 'I sold one just like it last week for 400.'
scenario.speaker_context: Brecca, a dwarven gemcutter who opens every negotiation with a high figure then offers a 'generous discount.'

structure.pattern_description: The first numerical information — Brecca's 900-gold appraisal — sets a mental reference point that distorts evaluation of subsequent prices. Her 600-gold offer feels like a deal only because it is compared to the anchor, not to the actual market value (~400g).
structure.formal_form: Initial anchor A (900g) is introduced. Offer O (600g) is framed as O << A, triggering bargain perception, even when O >> true value V (~400g).
structure.why_wrong: The 900-gold figure is arbitrary or inflated, yet it shapes the buyer's sense of what is reasonable. Judging 600 as a good price depends on accepting the anchor rather than independently estimating worth.
structure.counterpoint: Anchoring is not always irrational — when the anchor is a genuinely informative signal from a trusted authority, using it is reasonable. The error lies in treating an arbitrary or strategically chosen number as meaningful.

assessment.identification_prompt: Brecca's offer of 600 gold feels like a bargain. What is influencing that feeling, and should you trust it?

rubric.description: Accepts the deal at face value; sees 600 gold as a genuine discount.
Senses something is off but cannot articulate why the 900-gold figure matters.
Recognizes the 900-gold appraisal makes 600 seem cheap by comparison, but does not generalize.
Identifies that the initial high number is setting a reference point that distorts judgment, notes the need for independent estimates.
Clearly explains anchoring, distinguishes the anchor from genuine market evidence, and suggests strategies like researching prices independently.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: If Brecca had simply said '600 gold' with no other number mentioned, would the price feel the same? What changed?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Now suppose you are the one selling. How could you use this technique ethically — or is any deliberate anchor manipulative?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Brecca is cheerful and fast-talking. She drops high numbers casually and watches for the buyer's reaction before swooping in with her 'special price.'
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Ah, you've got a keen eye! That fire opal was appraised at nine hundred gold by the Guild. But between you and me, let's call it six hundred and shake on it.
game_hooks.resolution_path: If the player identifies anchoring and negotiates using the 400-gold reference, Brecca laughs, concedes ~420 gold, and respects the player's savvy.

scenario.context: You have entered the Arcanum Research Lab to assist with a crucial experiment on crystal energy yields. Dr. Selene Varr, the lead researcher, greets you at the central console.
scenario.text: "Our preliminary scan shows the new quartz batch can produce up to **1,200 units** of raw energy per hour," Dr. Varr announces, pointing to a glowing readout. "Given that, I think we can safely allocate **900 units** to the upcoming field test and still have plenty left for backup. What do you think?" Behind her, a junior researcher whispers, "Last batch of similar crystals only managed about **650 units** under the same conditions."
scenario.speaker_context: Dr. Selene Varr is confident and persuasive, always leading with the most optimistic figure from a single test before discussing allocations.

structure.pattern_description: Dr. Varr introduces an inflated initial figure (1,200 units) which becomes the reference point for all subsequent judgments. The player’s decision to allocate 900 units feels reasonable only because it is compared to the high anchor, not to the more realistic historical yield (~650 units).
structure.formal_form: Anchor A = 1,200; Proposed allocation P = 900; True typical yield T ≈ 650. Decision bias occurs when P is judged acceptable because P << A, despite P > T.
structure.why_wrong: The 1,200‑unit figure comes from an outlier measurement and is presented without context, causing the player to overestimate the batch's capability and allocate more energy than the crystals can reliably produce.
structure.counterpoint: Anchoring can be useful when the initial number is a reliable benchmark from a trusted source; it speeds up decision‑making. The error here is that the anchor is an atypical, optimistic outlier rather than a solid reference.

assessment.identification_prompt: Why does allocating 900 units feel like a safe choice, and what hidden influence might be shaping that impression?

rubric.description: Accepts the 900‑unit allocation without question, treating it as the only logical option.
Feels uneasy about the allocation but cannot explain why the initial 1,200‑unit figure matters.
Notes that the 1,200‑unit number makes 900 seem modest, but does not connect it to past data.
Identifies the initial 1,200‑unit figure as an anchor that skews perception of the 900‑unit offer, and mentions the earlier 650‑unit reference.
Fully explains anchoring, distinguishes the outlier anchor from typical yields, and proposes checking multiple test results before deciding on the allocation.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: If the player accepts the allocation, Dr. Varr’s experiment fails, producing only 660 units and forcing a costly emergency shutdown. The lab director then explains that the initial 1,200‑unit reading was a single spike, prompting the player to reflect on how the first number biased their judgment.
assessment.follow_up_if_right: If the player questions the anchor, Dr. Varr provides additional test logs showing a range of 620‑680 units. The player then suggests allocating 700 units, preserving a safety margin. The experiment succeeds, and the player earns a “Critical Thinker” badge.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Confident, data‑driven, but prone to highlight best‑case scenarios; enjoys impressing newcomers with impressive numbers.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Our latest scan indicates a peak output of ... Based on that, we can safely set aside ... I’ve seen higher numbers in a few trials, so we’re in good shape.
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player can either (a) accept the suggested allocation, (b) request additional data, or (c) propose an alternative allocation based on historical averages. Each path leads to a distinct outcome and a debrief on anchoring.

scenario.context: You are leading a caravan across the Sunfire Plains, searching for the next fuel stop before nightfall.
scenario.text:
A weathered road‑guide named Jorin steps out from a dusty roadside shack. "Listen, friend," he says, "the main depot at Dustwind Oasis is charging a steep $5.00 per gallon these days. I know a guy who can sell you a barrel for $3.50 right here. It’s a solid deal, especially with the sun beating down."

A fellow traveler passing by mutters, "I refueled at Dustwind last week for $2.80 a gallon."

Jorin leans in and adds, "That was before the recent drought. Prices have gone up. Trust me, $3.50 is a bargain now."
scenario.speaker_context: Jorin, a seasoned but opportunistic road‑guide who always opens his pitch with the highest recent price he can recall, then frames his own offer as a discount.

structure.pattern_description: Jorin first mentions a high reference price ($5.00 per gallon). That figure becomes the mental anchor, making his $3.50 offer feel like a good deal even though the true market price is lower (~$2.80). The player's judgment about the fairness of the price is distorted by the initial anchor.
structure.why_wrong: The $5.00 figure is exaggerated and not reflective of the current market. By presenting it first, Jorin skews the player's perception, causing them to overvalue the $3.50 price relative to the actual baseline.
structure.counterpoint: Anchoring can be useful when the initial figure comes from a reliable source, such as an official price board. In that case, using it as a reference helps make quick decisions. The error here is that the anchor is deliberately inflated to manipulate judgment.

assessment.identification_prompt: You feel that $3.50 per gallon is a great discount after hearing Jorin mention $5.00. What mental shortcut is influencing your feeling, and how should you verify the true price?

rubric.description: Accepts the $3.50 price without questioning the $5.00 figure.
Feels uneasy about the deal but cannot explain why the $5.00 number matters.
Notes that the $5.00 price sets a reference point, making $3.50 seem cheap, but does not consider checking actual market rates.
Identifies anchoring as the cause of the perceived bargain and suggests looking up recent fuel prices before deciding.

Clearly explains how the initial $5.00 anchor skews judgment, compares it to the observed $2.80 price, and proposes concrete actions (e.g., ask for recent price list, consult a map, or wait for an official price sign) to avoid the bias.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: If the player accepts the deal, Jorin later reveals the true price was $2.80, and the player loses extra gold. Use this outcome to discuss how the initial high figure anchored their perception and how checking independent sources could have prevented the loss.
assessment.follow_up_if_right: If the player asks for a recent price list or decides to wait for the official depot sign, they discover the $2.80 rate and either negotiate a better price or travel directly to Dustwind Oasis, saving gold and reinforcing the value of questioning anchors.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Jorin is charismatic, quick‑talking, and eager to profit; he frames information to sound helpful while subtly steering decisions.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed:
You know, the last time I checked, the depot was charging a steep five bucks per gallon. Prices have jumped since then.
I can get you a barrel for three‑fifty – that's a solid discount, especially with the heat beating down.
Don't worry about the price chase; I’ve got the best deal on this stretch.
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player can (a) accept Jorin's offer, (b) request a recent price reference, (c) ignore Jorin and continue to the official depot. Each choice leads to a different outcome that highlights the anchoring effect.

scenario.context: You are a newly inducted apprentice in the Guild Apprentice Workshop. The master has tasked you with acquiring a rare embersteel ingot for the upcoming Mastercraft ceremony. Two vendors are present in the workshop courtyard: Grunthor, a dwarf smith known for flamboyant sales pitches, and Lira, a human trader who specializes in joint‑purchase agreements.
scenario.text:
Grunthor brandishes a glowing embersteel ingot and shouts, "This masterpiece? Certified by the Iron Guild at 1,200 gold! But for a sharp-eyed apprentice like you, I’ll let it go for 800 gold — a steal, I tell you!" A nearby apprentice whispers, "I heard the market price is only about 500 gold.

Lira steps forward and says, "If you and I pool our gold we can buy two ingots from the distant forge and split the surplus. My outside deal would give me a surplus of 120 gold, yours would give you a surplus of 80 gold. The total surplus from the joint purchase is 200 gold. How shall we divide it fairly?"
scenario.speaker_context: Grunthor opens negotiations with an inflated anchor price, then offers a “discount.” Lira proposes a collaborative trade and stresses fairness based on each party’s outside options.

structure.pattern_description: Grunthor’s 1,200‑gold appraisal serves as an anchor that makes his 800‑gold offer appear generous, even though the true market value is ~500 gold. Simultaneously, Lira’s bargaining scenario requires the apprentice to apply a fairness (Nash bargaining) analysis, using each party’s outside‑option surplus (120 g for Lira, 80 g for the apprentice) to determine a mutually beneficial split of the 200‑gold joint surplus.
structure.formal_form: Anchor A = 1,200g, Offer O = 800g, True value V ≈ 500g. Fair split S_i = Outside_i + (TotalSurplus - ΣOutside) * (Outside_i / ΣOutside).
structure.why_wrong: A common error is to accept Grunthor’s 800‑gold price because the anchor makes it feel like a discount, and to split the 200‑gold surplus equally (100/100) without accounting for the differing outside options, leading to an unfair allocation.
structure.why_right: Recognize the anchoring bias, compare the offer to the market price, and negotiate a lower price (≈500 g). Then calculate a fair division of the joint surplus using each party’s fallback surplus, yielding Lira 120 g + (200‑200)*(120/200)=120 g and Apprentice 80 g + (200‑200)*(80/200)=80 g, i.e., a 120/80 split.
structure.counterpoint: If the apprentice ignores the anchor and insists on the market price, Grunthor may refuse to sell, forcing the apprentice to rely on Lira’s joint purchase—demonstrating how anchoring can also affect bargaining power.

assessment.identification_prompt: Identify the anchoring figure in Grunthor’s pitch and explain why it is misleading. Then, using the outside‑option surpluses (120 g for Lira, 80 g for you), compute the fair split of the 200‑gold joint surplus.

rubric.description: No correct identification of either concept.
Mentions one concept but provides no reasoning.
Identifies one concept but misses the other.
Identifies both anchoring and bargaining fairness but does not integrate them.
Correctly identifies the anchor, explains its bias, calculates the fair split using outside options, and describes how the two concepts interact.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Hint: Compare Grunthor’s 800‑gold offer to the known market price of 500 gold. Then recall the Nash bargaining formula that weights each party’s outside‑option surplus when dividing a joint surplus.
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Excellent! You’ve spotted the deceptive anchor and applied a fairness calculation. Use this insight to negotiate a better price with Grunthor and secure the optimal split with Lira.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Grunthor is boisterous, confident, and loves to brag about his numbers. Lira is pragmatic, cooperative, and values mutually beneficial deals.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Grunthor: "A price like this doesn’t come often—only for the keenest apprentices!" Lira: "Let’s make sure both of us walk away with what our alternatives would have given us, plus a share of the extra value we create together."
game_hooks.resolution_path: If the player negotiates the ingot down to ≤550 g, Grunthor becomes neutral and offers a small extra discount. If the player correctly splits the surplus 120/80, Lira rewards the apprentice with a bonus crafting material. Failure leads to paying the inflated price and missing the joint‑purchase bonus.

source.source_material: Integrated scenario: E1.3 (Anchoring), C4.1 (Bargaining and fairness)

scenario.context: The player arrives at the Cartographers' Guild in the city of Veranthos. The Guild is preparing an expedition to map the uncharted Thornveil Marshes. Master Cartographer Lirel has spent thirty years mapping difficult terrain and is reviewing applications from volunteers. The player witnesses an exchange between Lirel and a young applicant named Dax, who completed a six-week surveying course last month.
scenario.text: Dax spreads a hand-drawn map on the table with a flourish. 'I mapped the entire Greenvale basin in two weeks. My instructor said it was the fastest anyone had finished the exercise. I'm ready for the Thornveil.' Lirel studies the map quietly, then says: 'Your contour lines assume uniform slope between your sample points. The Thornveil has karst sinkholes — the ground drops thirty feet with no surface warning. How would you handle that?' Dax barely pauses: 'Same technique, just more sample points. It's all just measurement at the end of the day.' Lirel turns to the player with a weary expression. 'Bertrand Russell once wrote that the trouble with the world is that the stupid are cocksure and the intelligent are full of doubt. I would not call young Dax stupid, but I would note that I have mapped eleven marshlands, and the more I map, the less certain I am that I know what I am doing.'
scenario.speaker_context: Lirel is not being arrogant — she genuinely recognizes how much she still does not know about difficult terrain. Dax is not dishonest — he genuinely believes his six weeks of training have given him sufficient competence, because he does not yet know enough to see what he is missing.

structure.pattern_description: Dax's limited training gives him confidence because he cannot yet see the complexities he has not encountered. His map of Greenvale worked because Greenvale was simple terrain; he generalizes from this success to assume the Thornveil will be the same. Lirel's decades of experience have taught her how many ways mapping can go wrong, which makes her more cautious, not less. The asymmetry: low competence produces high confidence because the knowledge needed to recognize one's own gaps is the same knowledge one lacks.
structure.formal_form: Agent with low competence in domain D overestimates their competence because recognizing the limits of their knowledge requires the very knowledge they lack. Agent with high competence in D underestimates their relative standing because they assume others share their awareness of D's difficulties.
structure.why_wrong: Dax's confidence is not based on evidence that his methods will work in the Thornveil — it is based on his inability to imagine how they might fail. He does not know what karst terrain does to contour assumptions because he has never encountered it. His confidence is inversely proportional to his awareness of the problem space.
structure.counterpoint: Confidence and competence do sometimes align. A skilled person can be justifiably confident. The Dunning-Kruger pattern is specifically about the metacognitive gap: the inability to evaluate one's own performance accurately when one lacks the relevant expertise. It is not a claim that all confident people are incompetent.

assessment.identification_prompt: Dax seems eager and confident. Lirel seems cautious and uncertain. If you had to choose one of them to lead you into the Thornveil Marshes, who would you pick, and why? What does Lirel's uncertainty tell you that Dax's certainty does not?

rubric.description: Player picks Dax because he sounds more confident, or sees Lirel's caution as a sign of weakness.
Player picks Lirel based on experience but cannot articulate why Dax's confidence is misleading.
Player recognizes that Dax's confidence outstrips his experience and that Lirel's caution comes from deeper knowledge, but does not articulate the metacognitive mechanism.
Player identifies the Dunning-Kruger pattern: Dax is confident because he does not know enough to see what he is missing, while Lirel's doubt reflects awareness of genuine complexity.

Player identifies the Dunning-Kruger effect, explains the metacognitive gap (the knowledge needed to see your limits is the knowledge you lack), connects it to Russell's quote, and can describe conditions under which confidence would be a reliable signal of competence.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Think about what Dax's training covered and what it did not. He mapped a gentle valley in good conditions. What does that experience teach him about sinkholes, shifting water tables, or terrain that changes overnight? If he has never encountered those problems, how would he know to worry about them?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Here is the harder question: how do you tell the difference between Lirel's healthy expert humility and simple lack of confidence? If doubt can be a sign of competence, how do you avoid the opposite error — dismissing every confident person as a Dax?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Dax is enthusiastic, earnest, and slightly defensive when questioned. He genuinely wants to help and does not realize his overconfidence is dangerous. Lirel is quiet, precise, and faintly amused by youthful certainty because she remembers being exactly like Dax thirty years ago.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Dax grins as you approach: 'You here to sign up for the Thornveil expedition? It'll be great — I've got my methods dialed in. Six weeks of training and I mapped a whole valley. How hard can a marsh be?'
game_hooks.resolution_path: If the player identifies the Dunning-Kruger pattern, Lirel nods approvingly and assigns the player to mentor Dax on the expedition's advance team. Dax initially resists but, after encountering his first sinkhole and realizing his contour method failed completely, becomes genuinely curious about what else he does not know. Lirel rewards the player with a Guild surveying kit and the observation: 'The most dangerous moment in any craft is when you first feel competent.'

scenario.context: The player arrives at the frontier village of Brindlewick, a newly settled community on the edge of the Great River. The village is suffering from a seasonal drought, and the council has approved a project to dig a new irrigation ditch to bring water from the river to the fields. Elder Mara, the village's seasoned watermaster who has spent twenty years managing the river's flow, is reviewing the project plans. A young farmer named Jorin, who finished a two‑week apprenticeship in basic irrigation last month, steps forward to present his own design.
scenario.text: "I read the whole manual in a single night," Jorin declares, spreading a crude sketch of a straight trench across the table. "I can dig it myself in three days, and the water will flow straight to the crops. No need for fancy gates or slope calculations—just dig and fill!" Elder Mara studies the sketch, then replies, "A straight ditch will quickly fill with silt, and without proper gradient the water will pool and ruin the fields. How will you handle the river's seasonal rise and the rocky outcrop three furlongs downstream?" Jorin smiles confidently, "I’ll just dig a little deeper there. The same method works everywhere, right?"
scenario.speaker_context: Elder Mara is not dismissive; she is deeply aware of the many variables that affect irrigation and knows her own limits. Jorin genuinely believes his brief training has given him sufficient mastery, because he has not yet encountered the complexities of real-world water management.

structure.pattern_description: Jorin's limited apprenticeship gives him unwarranted confidence; he cannot see the hidden challenges of irrigation because he lacks the experience needed to recognize them. Elder Mara's decades of practice have shown her how many ways a simple ditch can fail, which makes her cautious rather than overconfident. The asymmetry: low competence produces high confidence because the knowledge required to detect one's own gaps is the same knowledge one lacks.
structure.why_wrong: Jorin assumes that because a simple trench worked in his textbook example, the same approach will succeed in the village's varied terrain. He overlooks essential factors such as slope, soil composition, water flow rate, and seasonal variability—issues that only experience with real projects can reveal. His confidence stems from not yet knowing what he does not know.
structure.counterpoint: Elder Mara could invite Jorin to assist on a smaller, supervised section of the ditch, allowing him to observe the impact of gradient and soil type first-hand, thereby calibrating his confidence with concrete experience.

assessment.identification_prompt: Which cognitive bias is illustrated by Jorin's belief that his brief training is enough to design and build the irrigation ditch?

rubric.description: No identification of the bias; response is unrelated.
Names a bias but it is incorrect or vague.
Correctly identifies the Dunning‑Kruger effect but provides no explanation.
Identifies the Dunning‑Kruger effect and explains why Jorin exhibits it.
Provides a thorough explanation, connects it to the scenario details, and suggests a concrete mitigation strategy for the player.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: The player receives a hint: "Consider how Jorin’s limited experience might be influencing his confidence about the ditch’s design."
assessment.follow_up_if_right: The player is praised and offered a chance to mentor Jorin, unlocking a side quest that improves the village’s irrigation system.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Elder Mara is patient, pragmatic, and values learning through hands‑on experience. Jorin is enthusiastic, proud, and eager to prove himself.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: "I respect your enthusiasm, Jorin, but the river does not obey our wishes without careful planning..."
game_hooks.resolution_path: If the player advises Jorin to join a supervised trial dig, the project succeeds, gaining village reputation and a modest resource reward. If the player ignores the bias, the ditch fails, leading to crop loss and a lesson about overconfidence.

scenario.context: The player enters the busy West Wing of Saint Aurelia Hospital during a night shift. The ward is short-staffed, and a senior doctor, Dr. Maren Voss, is overseeing the team. A newly hired nurse practitioner, Lila, has just completed a two‑week orientation and is eager to prove herself.
scenario.text: Lila approaches Dr. Voss with a stack of patient charts. 'Doctor, I’ve read the protocol for insulin drip titration, and I’m confident I can adjust the rates on my own tonight. I’ve already set up the pumps for three patients without any issues.' Dr. Voss glances at the charts, noting that two of the patients have fluctuating renal function and one is on a beta‑blocker. She replies, 'That’s great enthusiasm, Lila, but the protocol for those cases includes additional lab checks and a physician’s sign‑off before any change.' Lila smiles, 'I’ll just follow the standard chart I used for the other patients. It’s the same drug, same dosage, just a different chart.' The player can choose to (A) let Lila proceed alone, (B) intervene and ask her to wait for a physician’s order, or (C) ask Lila to explain how the renal function and beta‑blocker interaction affect insulin dosing.
scenario.speaker_context: Dr. Voss is experienced and aware of the nuances of insulin management in complex patients. Lila genuinely believes her brief training is sufficient, because she has not yet encountered a case where the standard protocol fails. She is not being deceptive, just overconfident due to limited experience.

structure.pattern_description: Lila’s limited exposure to insulin management leads her to overestimate her competence, assuming that because she successfully set up simple drips, she can handle more complicated cases without supervision. The senior doctor’s humility stems from decades of encountering edge cases that reveal hidden complexities.
structure.formal_form: Agent with low competence in domain D overestimates their ability because they lack the meta‑knowledge required to recognize their gaps. Agent with high competence underestimates their relative expertise, assuming others share their awareness of D’s subtleties.
structure.why_wrong: Lila’s confidence is not based on evidence that her approach will be safe for patients with renal impairment or interacting medications. She cannot see the risks she lacks knowledge of, so her decision could lead to hypoglycemia or other adverse events.
structure.counterpoint: When might this heuristic be useful? In low‑stakes situations where rapid action is needed and the cost of hesitation outweighs the risk of a small error, overconfidence can keep momentum.

assessment.identification_prompt: Which character’s behavior best illustrates the Dunning‑Kruger effect, and why?

rubric.description: No identification or incorrect character identified.
Identifies Lila but provides an incomplete or inaccurate explanation of the bias.
Identifies Lila and mentions overconfidence, but does not connect it to her limited knowledge.
Correctly identifies Lila, explains that her brief training prevents her from recognizing her knowledge gaps, and contrasts with Dr. Voss’s humility.
Provides a thorough analysis, citing specific details (renal function, beta‑blocker interaction) that Lila overlooks, and explains how the bias could impact patient safety.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: The player is prompted to review Lila’s chart notes and a brief tutorial on how expertise gaps can inflate confidence, then asked to reassess the situation.
assessment.follow_up_if_right: The player receives praise from Dr. Voss and unlocks a ‘Critical Thinking’ skill point for recognizing the Dunning‑Kruger effect.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Lila is eager, talkative, and eager to prove herself; Dr. Voss is measured, patient, and cautious.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Lila: 'I’ve got this, doctor. I’ve already done it twice.' / Dr. Voss: 'Confidence is good, but let’s double‑check the labs first.'

scenario.context: The player is in the port town of Saltmere, where the Town Watch is debating how to allocate its limited patrol budget for the next quarter. Captain Voss has called a meeting after two dramatic wolf attacks on the coastal road last month. The Watch has data showing that pickpocketing in the market district accounts for ten times more losses than wolf attacks over the past year, but the wolf attacks were violent and widely discussed.
scenario.text: Captain Voss addresses the Watch. 'We all know what happened on the coastal road. Farmer Brek nearly lost his arm. His daughter still won't leave the house. I'm proposing we double the coastal road patrols and station archers at the Ridgeline overlook. That means pulling four officers from the market district, but the wolves are the real threat right now.' Sergeant Tully clears her throat. 'Captain, I pulled the ledger. We've had two wolf attacks this year, both last month. We've had a hundred and fourteen pickpocketing incidents in the market district in the same period. The market losses total eight times the value of livestock lost to wolves.' Voss frowns. 'Numbers on a page, Tully. I can still hear Brek screaming. The people of Saltmere need to feel safe, and right now they're terrified of wolves, not pickpockets.'
scenario.speaker_context: Captain Voss is not incompetent — he is responding to genuine fear in the community. But his resource allocation decision is being driven by the vividness and emotional salience of the wolf attacks rather than by the actual frequency and magnitude of threats.

structure.pattern_description: Voss is judging the probability and severity of threats based on how easily examples come to mind. The wolf attacks are vivid, recent, emotionally charged, and widely discussed — making them highly 'available' in memory. Pickpocketing is mundane, individually minor, and forgettable. This asymmetry in mental availability distorts his risk assessment and drives a misallocation of resources.
structure.formal_form: Agent judges frequency or probability of event type E based on the ease with which instances of E come to mind, rather than on actual base rates. Vivid, recent, or emotionally charged events are overweighted; routine, statistical, or undramatic events are underweighted.
structure.why_wrong: Two wolf attacks versus 114 pickpocketing incidents and an 8:1 loss ratio clearly indicate where the greater harm lies. Voss acknowledges the data and dismisses it because his emotional memory of the attacks feels more real than the statistics. The result is a resource allocation that protects against the rare dramatic threat while leaving the common undramatic threat unaddressed.
structure.counterpoint: Emotional salience is not always misleading. If the wolf attacks signal a new pattern (e.g., wolves driven from their territory by drought), the frequency data from the past year may understate the future risk. The error is not in taking vivid events seriously, but in letting vividness substitute for frequency analysis.

assessment.identification_prompt: Captain Voss has data from Sergeant Tully showing the market district is a much bigger problem. Why does he still want to prioritize the coastal road? What is driving his judgment if not the numbers?

rubric.description: Player agrees with Voss that wolves are the priority because the attacks were scary.
Player senses Voss might be overreacting but frames it as an emotional decision rather than a cognitive pattern.
Player identifies that Voss is weighting the dramatic events over the statistical evidence but does not name or describe the underlying mechanism.
Player identifies the availability heuristic: Voss judges threat severity by how easily and vividly the wolf attacks come to mind, overriding the base-rate data.

Player identifies the availability heuristic, explains the role of vividness, recency, and emotional charge in distorting risk assessment, and can articulate when emotional salience might legitimately signal a real change in threat level.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Imagine you had never heard about the wolf attacks and you were just looking at the ledger numbers. Where would you put the patrols? Now ask yourself: what changed when you added the story of Farmer Brek?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Good. Now consider Voss's point about public feeling: 'The people need to feel safe.' Is there a legitimate reason to allocate some resources based on perceived rather than actual risk? Where is the line between good leadership and bad reasoning?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Captain Voss is a brave, sincere leader who takes his duty to protect Saltmere personally. He is not stupid but he trusts his gut over spreadsheets. He becomes defensive when he feels his judgment is being questioned by 'desk work.'
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: You weren't there when we pulled Brek off that road. I was. I don't need a ledger to tell me what's dangerous in my town.
game_hooks.resolution_path: If the player identifies the availability heuristic, Sergeant Tully backs them up with the data. Voss, after some resistance, agrees to a compromise: maintain current coastal patrols but do not strip the market district. He later admits to the player that he had been having nightmares about the wolf attacks and realizes that was coloring his judgment.

scenario.context: The player arrives in the bustling market district of Rivermist during the annual Festival of Lanterns. While strolling through the flower stalls, they encounter Lira, a well‑known local matchmaker who runs a tiny booth adorned with rose petals and love charms.
scenario.text:
"Oh, traveler! You must be careful where you look for a partner tonight," Lira says, eyes wide. "Just yesterday, a handsome merchant from the Midnight Bazaar charmed a young scholar, only to vanish with her purse and a love‑letter full of false promises. The whole tavern is still buzzing about it—people are calling it the 'Midnight Scam.' I advise you to avoid the Bazaar entirely and stick to the town square where the folk are honest and predictable."
The player can either:
1. Accept Lira's advice and only approach potential dates in the town square.
2. Question Lira about the overall success rate of matches from the Bazaar versus the square.
3. Ignore the warning and mingle freely, including at the Bazaar.
scenario.speaker_context: Lira is genuinely trying to protect the player from a painful experience, but her recommendation is driven by the vivid, recent scandal rather than the long‑term statistics that show 73% of successful matches in Rivermist originated from the Bazaar, while only 28% came from the town square.

structure.pattern_description: Lira judges the safety and suitability of dating locations based on the ease with which the recent scandal at the Midnight Bazaar comes to mind, overweighting that vivid episode and underweighting the broader, less memorable data about successful matches.
structure.formal_form: Agent evaluates the probability or desirability of event type E based on the mental availability of recent, vivid instances of E, ignoring base‑rate statistics.
structure.why_wrong: The single scandal, though dramatic, is statistically insignificant compared to the overall success record of the Bazaar. By letting the recent story dominate her judgment, Lira steers the player away from the most fertile dating ground, potentially missing out on better matches.
structure.counterpoint: When might this heuristic be useful? In situations where quick decisions are needed and recent vivid events are indeed strong indicators of current risk (e.g., an ongoing outbreak of a contagious disease).

assessment.identification_prompt: Which cognitive bias is Lira displaying when she advises the player to avoid the Midnight Bazaar based on the recent scandal?

rubric.description: No recognition of the bias; response unrelated.
Mentions a bias but selects the wrong one (e.g., confirmation bias).
Identifies the correct bias label but cannot explain why it applies.
Correctly names the Availability heuristic and gives a brief reason tied to the vivid scandal.
Fully articulates the heuristic, links it to Lira's decision, contrasts it with the base‑rate data, and notes potential consequences for the player.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Lira sighs, "I understand why you might think otherwise, but let me tell you about the many happy couples that met at the Bazaar. The recent tale is just a whisper among many successes. Consider looking at the records before deciding."
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Lira smiles, "Exactly. The story spreads fast, but the numbers tell a different tale. Use both the stories and the statistics to make a wiser choice."

game_hooks.npc_personality: Charismatic, well‑meaning, slightly melodramatic; loves gossip and sees herself as a guardian of hearts.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed:
Did you hear about the merchant who vanished with the scholar's purse?
The Bazaar is full of charm, but also of tricksters—just ask anyone who was there last night.
People say love is safest where the streets are quiet and the lanterns are steady.
game_hooks.resolution_path: If the player chooses option 2, they unlock a hidden ledger showing match statistics, allowing them to make an informed decision. Choosing option 1 leads to fewer successful encounters, while option 3 opens a chance for a high‑reward romance but also the risk of encountering a swindler.
